The China export control argument becomes a recurring Eisman talking point, and the episode sets up the data center infrastructure deep dive with Nick Del Deo three weeks later.

quotes.q: The chances of that at some point happening, it has to be 100%. It's not now.
In my view he was delusionally optimistic.

questions: What observable capex behavior marks the start of the inevitable digestion period?
Does restricting Nvidia in China create the global Huawei competitor Rasgon fears, and how fast?
Can Lip-Bu Tan find foundry customers before Intel's balance sheet forces the question?

title: Inside America’s Economic Divide: AI, Tariffs, & The Fed | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 29
thesis: Liesman's core move is to separate what Eisman conflates: the market and the economy. The market is in a momentum fervor, as long as investors reward companies for raising AI investment, the investment continues, a loop he compares to the post-2000 period, while the economy underneath is genuinely K-shaped, with tariff-hit industries laying people off and their damage papered over by AI spending. He endorses watching auto loans as the stress gauge because economists know the car payment is the last bill a strapped consumer skips. His deeper argument, drawn from Fed history and his years running the Wall Street Journal's Moscow bureau, is institutional: markets only work inside societies that understand and accept price signals, which is why imposing a universal legal code on 1990s Russia failed while oil privatization worked, and why Fed credibility and communication matter as much as rate decisions.
pushback: The pushback runs unusually in both directions. Eisman opens with his twitch: 29.18 trillion of GDP growing 1.8% is about 530 billion dollars, and with 400 billion plus of AI capex the rest of the economy is flat, and Liesman's first two answers are corrections, telling him he is mixing the market up with the economy. Eisman counters with the Henry Blodget story: across the hall at Oppenheimer in the late 90s, Blodget was 1,000% right that the internet would change the world and create dynastic wealth, and investors still got carried out, his standing objection to trillions-in-returns talk from Jensen Huang. On the Fed, Eisman presses that what people brought Greenspan was ethics and fraud and he stood aside; Liesman defends Greenspan as an enigma who improved communication but concedes nothing on the ethics point.
evidence: US GDP of 29.18 trillion dollars in 2024 with consensus 2025 growth of 1.8% implies roughly 530 billion dollars of growth
Hyperscaler AI spending above 400 billion dollars leaves the economy outside AI essentially flat
Orvis is closing stores and laying off workers as tariffs hit fishing gear importers on both the import duty and metal content
The US government paid accounting firms millions of dollars to write a universal legal code for Russia, which failed
Within two years of privatization, Russian oil companies reversed a 20 year decline in Soviet oil output
The Fed in 1929 saw excess speculation but would not raise rates for fear the institution would not survive, then failed to flood the system with liquidity in 1930 to 1933
shift: Eisman accepts the market-versus-economy distinction as the better frame for his own K-shaped data but keeps the twitch, and Liesman explicitly validates the K-shaped label for the tariff economy. Neither yields on Greenspan: Eisman holds the ethics indictment, Liesman the institutionalist defense. The shared landing spot is that AI returns are unknowable this early and the Blodget precedent cuts both ways.
context: This is the episode where Eisman's GDP-minus-AI-capex arithmetic, first aired in the October 3 wrap, gets stress-tested by a professional Fed watcher and survives. It deepens the show's banks-and-Fed thread with firsthand Greenspan history and links the AI boom to the show's favorite cautionary structure: a true revolution that still wrecked investors, the same frame Eisman brings to Sorkin's 1929 two weeks later.

quotes.q: The momentum will continue as long as the momentum continues.
He repeated that like 100 times, and you know what? He was 1,000% correct.
quotes.who: Steve Eisman, on Henry Blodget's internet call

questions: How long can market momentum reward AI capex before someone demands proof of returns?
If the car loan is the last bill consumers skip, how close is that indicator to flashing?
Would today's Fed act against speculation it can see, or repeat 1929's political paralysis?

title: The Next Revolution: AI, Advertising, and the Collapse of Old Media
thesis: The pair argue that the market keeps mispricing regulatory and technological risk. Their Apple sell case was never about fear, the world was not scared enough: a judge ruled Google's 20 billion dollars a year of search payments to Apple, 100% margin and about 20% of Apple's operating income, to be illegal monopolist conduct, and only a timid remedy preserved them, leaving Apple with the check but still no AI strategy. In telecom, fiber and cable are technically interchangeable, so the fiber overbuild wave funded by private equity at about 4,000 dollars per connected home is a returns problem, and distressed cable assets will eventually attract the same private equity money. In advertising, AI is a Christensen-style disruption that starts with small brands: Meta can turn a logo into fifteen fully produced, A/B tested ads in an afternoon, which armies of agency people cannot match. On AI capex itself they preach humility: the bull case is companies paying near-salary prices for bots that replace 125,000 dollar employees, the bear case is four competitors driving bot prices below what the infrastructure needs.
pushback: Eisman opens by framing the Apple story as fear that receded and Moffett immediately quibbles: investors were not scared to death and should have been. Eisman then presses the after-picture, Apple keeps the 20 billion but still has no discernible AI strategy, and offers his own clerk's-eye theory that the judge took the easy out because district judges hate being overturned. On Verizon he brings personal knowledge, noting new CEO Dan Schulman did not do a good job running PayPal, a stock he knows well, and the guests concede they know very little and are surmising. On AI returns Eisman keeps repeating the show's refrain, it is too early, you can dream any dream, there is no counterfactual, and drives the group to agree the burden of proof sits with Sam Altman.
evidence: Google pays Apple about 20 billion dollars a year, essentially 100% margin and roughly 20% of Apple's operating income, payments a judge ruled illegal before a mild remedy preserved them
A typical fiber overbuild costs about 4,000 dollars per connected home, roughly 2,300 dollars per home passed
Cable bears believe about 80% of the country will be overbuilt with fiber
Meta offers advertisers a fully produced TV ad from just a brand logo, A/B tested the same afternoon, with the 15 most effective versions by day's end
The AI bot bull case: a company replacing a 125,000 dollar employee should pay up to about 119,000 dollars for the bot
Verizon replaced its CEO with board member Dan Schulman, 67, formerly of PayPal
shift: Genuine convergence on humility: all three agree nobody can yet answer whether AI revenue supports the infrastructure spend, that near-term ROIC will not be pretty, and that the proof burden is Altman's. The guests hold their sector calls, agencies structurally doomed, cable oversold, streaming consolidation necessary, and Eisman holds Apple accountable for having no AI strategy despite the reprieve.
context: The episode fuses three show threads: AI capex and its returns get their most balanced bull-bear articulation yet, the Apple-Google antitrust saga previewed in the October 10 wrap resolves into a lesson about regulatory risk, and AI-driven job displacement enters the K-shaped economy story through advertising and youth unemployment. The bonus Del Deo data center episode days later extends the same firm's coverage into the infrastructure itself.

quotes.q: Those payments were essentially bribery. It was Google paying Apple not to be in the search business.
It's really on Sam Altman's shoulders to prove this makes sense.

questions: If bot prices get competed down, what level of AI revenue actually supports the infrastructure spend?
When does private equity start buying distressed cable at the coupon-clipping math Moffett describes?
Can the agency holding companies survive AI-generated advertising even as a shrunken business?

title: Inside the Data Center Boom: Understanding the Massive Infrastructure That Supports AI
thesis: Del Deo maps an industry where most of the action has left the public markets: only Digital Realty and Equinix remain listed because the capital required and the years of negative cash flow before payoff spooked public investors, pushing construction to private players and hyperscalers. The landlords are warehouses for computers, power, cooling, security; Equinix's real asset is connectivity, the on-ramp where networks, clouds and enterprises interconnect, so its AI payoff arrives when latency-sensitive apps and private AI deployments proliferate, like Bristol Myers putting a private GPU cluster inside Equinix. GPU economics are the open question, CoreWeave depreciates them over six years and OpenAI signed a five year deal with two one year renewals, so the assets have life but a supply-constrained market flatters returns. His contrarian core: tight power supply is good for operators, because lifting the constraint would push returns back toward the cost of capital, and the hundreds-of-gigawatts demand projections contain heavy double counting.
pushback: Eisman plays translator and sceptic at once. He forces plain English throughout, mocking that bitcoin miners repurposing capacity for high performance computing was a sentence definitely in English, and makes Del Deo unpack it. He presses the REIT structure, if you pay out your cash flow, must you constantly raise capital to grow, which Del Deo concedes has been a sore point with investors. He asks straight whether the energy constraint will actually bind, drawing out the double counting point, and on Lumen's pivot-to-growth pitch he demands a verdict, and what do you think, getting the admission that Del Deo is skeptical the legacy decline can be outrun as fast as management claims.
evidence: Only two public data center REITs remain, Digital Realty and Equinix; others like CyrusOne were taken private, one by KKR and GIP
Hyperscalers are effectively four players, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta, investing in IT infrastructure at globally unmatched scale
CoreWeave depreciates its GPUs over six years
OpenAI, arguably the most sophisticated chip user, signed a five year CoreWeave deal with two one year renewal options
Projections of hundreds of gigawatts of data center demand contain substantial double counting and uncertainty
Cogent, at roughly a 1.5 billion dollar market cap, bought the old Sprint fiber network and repurposed it to sell wavelengths against Lumen and Zayo
shift: Eisman ends better informed rather than converted, and says so, calling it really informative and inviting a return visit. Del Deo holds his contrarian positions: operators should want power to stay tight, Equinix's AI moment is still ahead of it, legacy telco pivots deserve skepticism, and Cogent is his interesting pick despite admitting he has been wrong on it for a couple of years.
context: A direct extension of the AI capex thread from Ives, Rasgon and the Moffett Nathanson episode, this time from the landlord's side of the boom, and the source of the show's recurring point that data center demand forecasts are double counted. The observation that public markets will not fund negative cash flow buildouts connects to the show's private credit thread: the Morgan Stanley 2.9 trillion dollar funding estimate Eisman cited in the September 26 wrap has to come from somewhere.

quotes.q: A data center is basically a warehouse for computers.
If I were a data center operator, I'd want supply to remain tight, because that's my stick to get better pricing.

questions: What is the true economic life of a GPU, and what happens to CoreWeave-style models if it is shorter than six years?
Does abundant power eventually arrive and compress operator returns toward the cost of capital?
When AI applications finally proliferate, does the value migrate to connectivity hubs like Equinix as Del Deo expects?

title: Andrew Ross Sorkin on the Crash of 1929 & The Parallels We See Today | The Real Eisman Playbook
thesis: Sorkin argues 1929 matters because its mechanics are recurring, not antique: completely unregulated markets, crazy leverage, and elite pump-and-dump pools run so openly that the operators, the era's equivalent of a Davos guest list, mailed each other circulars describing the manipulation. The crash formula he distills is credit, leverage plus FOMO, enabled by a Federal Reserve that saw the speculation but would not raise rates for fear the young institution would be destroyed politically, then compounded the bust by failing to flood the system with liquidity from 1930 to 1933. The aftermath also rhymes: a 250 dollar a week outside lawyer from Queens ran the investigation that exposed the bankers, shined light, and still sent nobody to jail, exactly as after 2008. Built from eight years in archives rather than interviews, the book is his prequel to Too Big to Fail: the same masters-of-the-universe paradigm, shattered the same way.
pushback: Eisman's opening challenge is why write about people who are all really dead, which Sorkin answers with the archive method, letters that explain what interviews once did. The sharper exchange runs the other way: Eisman uses the book to indict his own 2008 mistake, he and his team assumed the government knew how bad it was, and Sorkin's AIG scene, where officials in the room are stunned to learn AIG is in trouble, proved they had no clue, which is why he did not short everything that moved. Eisman also keeps interrupting the 1929 narrative with I have heard this before, forcing the parallels, no jail time, captured regulators, political fear at the Fed, to be stated explicitly rather than implied.
evidence: The book took eight years, built from archival letters and library boxes that had never been indexed
Pool operators circulated written circulars describing their manipulations, some literally handed out on the street
The congressional investigator hired to examine the bankers was paid 250 dollars a week and sent no one to jail
The 1929 Fed saw excessive speculation but feared raising rates would destroy the institution, then failed to supply liquidity in 1930 to 1933
Google-era comparison aside, JP Morgan's Jack Morgan knew he was not his father and installed Thomas Lamont, a former journalist, as the real operator
In Sorkin's AIG scene, days after Lehman, senior officials did not know AIG was in trouble
shift: Eisman concedes something real and personal: reading the book corrected his model of 2008, the authorities were not knowingly slow, they were genuinely ignorant and out of bandwidth. Sorkin agrees they could not compute it. Both leave holding the parallel: unregulated corners of today's markets, from crypto leverage to private pools of capital, are running the 1929 formula of credit, leverage and FOMO.
context: Previewed in the September 26 wrap where Eisman branded the week shenanigans, chaos and revolutions and tied Binance's domicile-hopping to 1929-style red flags, this episode is the historical anchor for the show's crypto scepticism and its warnings about unregulated leverage. It is also the fifth author interview of the run and pairs naturally with the Liesman episode's Fed history: both ask whether institutions act against manias they can plainly see.

quotes.q: It would be like the guest list at Davos getting together to pump and dump a stock.
That was our actual mistake, why we didn't short everything that moved.

questions: Which of today's unregulated corners, crypto leverage or private pools, is running the closest copy of the 1929 formula?
Would today's Fed tighten against visible speculation, or repeat the political paralysis of 1929?
If the next crisis comes, does anyone go to jail this time, or does the Pecora pattern repeat again?

title: Inside the Cannabis Comeback: How One Company is Beating a Broken Market | The Real Eisman Playbook
thesis: The Glass House team argues they have already won the hardest game in cannabis: they are profitable as the low-cost greenhouse grower in California, the most competitive, lowest-price, most discerning market in the country, after an industry-wide capital binge circa 2018 ended in overcapacity and years of being left for dead when federal legalization never came. Their production cost of roughly 100 dollars per pound undercuts out-of-state growers whose customers pay sometimes multiples of California prices, and only two of five greenhouses on their 165 acre farm, 120 acres under glass, are productive, so capacity can scale without reinventing anything. The dream scenario is regulatory: Trump has twice posted favorably on medical cannabis and backed Florida's adult-use ballot measure, and any rescheduling or interstate commerce opening lets a proven low-cost operator sell into markets, domestic and eventually export, priced at five to six times California levels. Training at altitude, then throwing a knife into a pillow.
pushback: Eisman opens with unusual disclosure discipline: he is a recent shareholder, calls the position fairly speculative, and states on air that he is not there to pump and dump. His pressing is diligence-style: how exactly did you get to a 53% gross margin when almost no cannabis company makes money; what do out-of-state competitors' costs actually look like; and on the dream scenario he forces the arithmetic, if six greenhouses run, do I just multiply revenue by two plus efficiency gains? He also makes management walk through the federal scheduling regime from scratch and recount the ICE raid on their farm, drawing out that they hired the former ICE director Julie Myers Wood to make the workforce auditable rather than fight the enforcement.
evidence: Glass House's market cap is under 1 billion dollars and, unlike most of the industry, it makes money
Second quarter gross margin was 53% with an EBITDA margin around 18%; Eisman normalizes ROE to the mid to high teens
Production cost runs at roughly 100 dollars per pound in the lowest-price market in the country
The farm spans about 165 acres with 120 acres of greenhouse, and only two of five greenhouses are productive today
Out-of-state customers often pay multiples of California prices, and export markets like Germany and the UK can price at five to six times California
Trump posted positively on medical cannabis twice on Truth Social and backed Florida's adult-use Amendment 3 against DeSantis
After the ICE raid, the company hired Julie Myers Wood, ICE director under George W. Bush, to audit its workforce
shift: No adversarial gap to close: Eisman entered as a shareholder and leaves one, but the episode fixes the frame he wants viewers to hold, a profitable operator whose base business works today and whose upside is a regulatory option he refuses to handicap. Management concedes the dream scenario depends entirely on Washington while insisting the California cost position wins under any rules.
context: The show's first management interview and its most explicit conflict-of-interest disclosure, applying the Eisman playbook, unit economics first, policy taken as given, to a left-for-dead sector the way earlier episodes did to banks and healthcare. It also extends the K-shaped economy theme from the supply side: a real business that grew through a capital drought while AI absorbs every marginal investment dollar elsewhere.

quotes.q: If you can win in California, you can win everywhere else. The inverse is definitely not true.
I'm not here to pump and dump. This is a podcast that's dedicated to education.

questions: Does rescheduling or interstate commerce actually arrive, and which one unlocks the California export model first?
Can the roughly 100 dollar per pound cost advantage survive contact with scaled competition in other states?
How should investors size a position whose base case is modest and whose upside is a binary policy event?

title: The Private Credit Panic: Why Wall Street’s Big Winners are Now Losing | Real Eisman Playbook Ep 33
thesis: Schorr argues the alternative asset managers are in a question phase, not a broken story. After monster years in 2023 and 2024, investors are giving back gains because they are asking whether this is the beginning of a credit cycle, which would be a problem for firms that manage and lend enormous amounts of credit, and because slow monetizations have left spread-related earnings weak, with Apollo hit hardest since half its balance sheet is its own insurance book. He points at the market's internal contradiction: Goldman near 800 and high-yield spreads tightening daily say credit is fine, while the private credit stocks trade as if a cycle has begun, and one of those views has to give. Underneath, he still believes in the group because long duration liabilities and private markets diversification are what the end LP wants. The traditional managers remain the bad of his good, bad and ugly framework because technology came for them in the form of index funds and ETFs at 5 to 15 basis points, and not one of them thought to build a private markets business.
pushback: Eisman opens by forcing the paradox: secular growth stories, record fundraising every quarter, a market at all-time highs, and the stocks are down 15 to 33%, so what is going on. He then makes Schorr explain tokenization in plain English, saying not one in 2 million people can, and questions what tokenizing something like a building's rent rolls actually accomplishes. On Goldman, Eisman delivers the counterfactual that had it skipped the consumer adventure ten years ago, sold the private equity on its balance sheet and just raised funds, it would be much farther along; Schorr's punchline is that we would call that company Morgan Stanley.
evidence: In 2025 Blackstone is down 15%, Apollo down 25%, KKR down 21% and Blue Owl down 33% despite record fundraising
KKR was up about 80% in 2024 and 30 to 40% the year before, so some giveback was natural
A classic private equity fund runs roughly 7 to 10 years and targets 2 to 2.5 times multiple of invested capital
Index funds and ETFs deliver market returns for 5 to 15 basis points, and there are now more ETFs than there are stocks
Goldman trades near 800 dollars while high-yield spreads tighten daily, a combination Schorr says cannot coexist with a credit cycle
Jane Fraser's Citi exited consumer businesses where it had roughly 2% market share across 100 countries
shift: Neither side capitulates. Schorr holds his structural bull case on private markets while conceding it is very tough sledding for the traditional managers, and Eisman stays wary that the stocks are signaling something credit markets have not priced. They converge only on the logic that the equity market and the high-yield market cannot both be right.
context: The fullest treatment yet of the show's private credit theme, taped as the wraps track Tricolor, First Brands and other credit accidents that Eisman keeps noting did not originate in private credit. It sets up Chris Verrone's January rule that the bull market lasts as long as banks work and credit stays calm, and complements the year-end wrap where private credit fear is named one of 2025's four themes.

quotes.q: Goldman Sachs can be 800 dollars and high-yield spreads can tighten every day? That doesn't make sense. One of these things has to give.
You know what we'd call them? Morgan Stanley.

questions: Is the alts selloff the market sniffing out a real credit cycle, or just multiple compression after two euphoric years?
Which corrects first, tight high-yield spreads or falling private credit stocks?
Can tokenization create real liquidity in private assets, or does it just relabel the same illiquid cash flows?

title: Inside Publishing’s Big Shakeup: AI, TikTok & the Battle Ahead | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 34
thesis: The panel argues publishing has already lived through one revolution and is entering another. Distribution power moved to Amazon and social media, so a platform, measured first in follower counts, now gates entry for nonfiction authors regardless of expertise. The economics fragmented too: traditional deals pay 10 to 12% royalties on cover price while hybrid publishers split profits with authors at ratios like 70 to 30, and formats multiplied, with romantasy readers who started in self-published ebooks now buying deluxe print editions. AI is the next shock, but the panel's case for survival is that the industry's scarce assets are talent picking and community around authors, the same shift music made when albums became low-margin marketing for concerts and readers began buying the person, not just the book.
pushback: Eisman tests the platform rule with a hypothetical: the world's leading expert on an important historical topic who has no social media presence, and gets the uncomfortable answer that the numbers now come first. He then confronts the panel with his own experiment, asking ChatGPT for two essays on whether morality is absolute or relative in the voices of Alasdair MacIntyre and Richard Posner, and receiving in 30 seconds work he says would have taken him a month. The panel does not dispute the quality; their defense is that fiction demands plot, pacing and characterization working in concert, which is still hard to mimic.
evidence: Traditional nonfiction royalties run 10 to 12% of cover price, while hybrid publishers offer profit shares around 70% to the author
Publishers now screen nonfiction proposals on social media numbers; five to seven years ago a speaking circuit or course audience was enough
Jennifer Weiss reads 100 plus submissions a week looking for plot, pacing and characterization together
Eisman's ChatGPT prompt returned two polished essays in about 30 seconds on an obscure philosophy question
The panel cannot name a decade-scale cultural phenomenon moving books, on the order of Oprah's club or Harry Potter, in the last five years
Romantasy titles that began as self-published ebooks now sell as deluxe editions with etched end papers and maps
shift: Eisman closes convinced that AI is definitely changing the industry, like all industries. The publisher urges embracing change, and both agents hold onto talent picking as the durable human edge, telling authors to stay hopeful. No one disputes the direction of change, only whether curation survives it.
context: The first entry in the show's new series on how industries change, an idea Eisman credits on air to his wife Valerie, and a deliberate look at AI from the demand and diffusion side rather than the capex side that dominates the wraps. It pairs with the Navan episode the following week, where AI appears as a cost weapon inside a business model.

quotes.q: Thirty seconds later, two essays showed up. I couldn't believe it. They were so good.
We're talent pickers in the end.

questions: Does the social media platform requirement permanently lock genuine expertise out of nonfiction publishing?
Can hybrid profit-share models displace the 10 to 12% royalty standard at scale?
What would a bestseller-making cultural force even look like in a fragmented social media world?

title: Why It’s So Difficult For Companies to Go Public: A CFO Explains the Process | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 35
thesis: Butte argues that an IPO is the end of a multi-year maturation project, not a banking transaction. At the New York Stock Exchange she arrived in January 2004 to find an iconic institution whose financial reporting was a plug rather than a process, and it took until March 2006 to build the repeatable, auditable numbers a public company must produce quarter after quarter. Going public buys four things, a branding event, an acceleration of maturation, easier access to capital, and an acquisition currency, and a company should know which ones it actually needs; the NYSE needed maturation, not brand. At Navan she applies the same discipline to a travel and expense platform whose pitch is that AI collapses the cost structure, running the business with a fraction of the support staff of legacy competitors.
pushback: Eisman punctures the folk version of going public, hire some bankers, bing bang boom, and makes Butte walk through why the NYSE took over two years. He then asks what he calls an uncomfortable question about why the deal, priced at 25, traded the way it did, and pushes for the unsaid number on customer support headcount until Butte draws the disclosure line, repeating that she has not said that publicly while conceding Navan uses less than a tenth of the support staffing of an Amex GBT.
evidence: Butte became NYSE CFO in January 2004 and the IPO did not price until March 2006, over two years of preparation
Her framework: going public provides a branding event, accelerated maturation, easier access to capital and an acquisition currency
Navan handles its current business with about 3,000 employees
Butte estimates Amex GBT has 10 to 20 times Navan's customer support agents, and Navan has said it uses less than a tenth of that staffing
The Navan IPO priced at 25 dollars
Audit readiness came down to proving a repeatable process; the old NYSE numbers were a plug
shift: There is no disagreement to resolve. Eisman comes away endorsing the thesis that going public is far harder than investors assume, and Butte holds her disclosure boundaries on the numbers he probes. The episode ends with her wishing him luck with his health during chemotherapy.
context: Extends the industry-transformation series into market plumbing and gives the AI theme a demand-side face: AI as an internal cost advantage rather than capex. It lands in the same month the wraps observe that newly public high flyers on 70 times earnings cannot afford to disappoint on any metric, which is exactly the regime Navan entered at 25 dollars.

quotes.q: Most people just think you hire some bankers, you go public, bing bang boom. That is not what happened.
It's a little bit of pleasure and it's a lot of pain.

questions: Why did the Navan IPO trade the way it did after pricing at 25, and what does that say about the 2025 IPO window?
Can AI-light support staffing hold its cost advantage as Navan scales into bigger enterprise accounts?
Which of Butte's four IPO benefits still justifies being public when private capital is so abundant?

title: Steve Eisman Reflects on 2008, The Big Short & Today’s K-Shaped Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 36
thesis: In a Case Western student forum moderated by Ivy Zelman, Eisman compresses his crisis account and applies it to today. The 2008 story was a debt story: credit default swaps written between systemically important firms tied their balance sheets into a spiderweb so complicated nobody knew where it began or ended, which is why AIG's 50 to 70 billion of CDS sold to the street forced a bailout. Today those same institutions are safe because deleveraging was so extreme, Citigroup going from at least 35 to 1 to 10 to 1, so the systemic anxiety has migrated to private credit, where he says he has no data showing a problem. On the current market he accepts that AI carries most of GDP growth and concedes the bubble worry has real validity, while dismissing housing as an investment that at best keeps pace with inflation.
pushback: The pressure runs in reverse: students press Eisman. One argues the fundamentals are weaker than the tape, with AI at almost 50% of GDP growth, China holding the rare earth cards, inflation and unemployment ticking up and shaky monetary policy, and asks whether an AI bubble is holding everything up; Eisman corrects the number upward, saying he thinks AI's share of growth is more than 50%, and concedes there is a lot of validity to the worry. Zelman also presses her own crisis villain, Greenspan's 2004 endorsement of ARMs plus the rating agencies, alongside Eisman's incentives story.
evidence: AIG sold roughly 50 to 70 billion dollars of credit default swaps to the street, the reason the government bailed it out
Citigroup was levered at least 35 to 1 before the crisis versus about 10 to 1 afterward, which Eisman calls the distance from Pluto to the sun
From 2002 through 2006 better-than-expected delinquencies led subprime lenders to loosen every year until the standard was can you breathe
A student cites AI as almost 50% of GDP growth; Eisman answers that he thinks it is more
Silicon Valley Bank's model was taking in Silicon Valley deposits and buying Treasuries for the spread, a liquidity story rather than a capital one
Eisman puts pre-crisis subprime shorting costs and the CDS mechanics in context of trillions in interbank derivative exposure
shift: Eisman gives more explicit ground on the AI bubble question than he does in studio, agreeing the skeptical case has a lot of validity, while holding firm that the banks are safe and that nothing in the data yet condemns private credit. Zelman keeps her Greenspan indictment; the two accounts of 2008 sit side by side rather than merging.
context: The live-audience rehearsal of the two-part 2008 masterclass posted over the following weeks, with the K-shaped economy, private credit and housing affordability themes all surfacing in the Q&A. It also delivers the show's most personal Big Short material, including his single contribution to the movie, the word schmuck.

quotes.q: I don't think housing is an investment anymore.
It was Greenspan. I blame him and the credit agencies.

questions: If AI is more than half of GDP growth, what happens to the real economy when that capex normalizes?
What data could settle whether private credit has a problem before losses actually arrive?
Does the banks-are-safe case survive a private credit shock that flows back through bank lending to the sector?

title: Inside the Industrial Comeback & AI’s Power Crisis with Nigel Coe | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 37
thesis: Coe's argument is that the industrial sector has split in two: pockets of growth and a lot of no growth, and the dividing line is the data center. Anything touching the AI buildout, electrical equipment, HVAC, gas turbines, is growing fast, while short cycle industrials have been stagnant for three years with the ISM stuck below 50. Power is the binding constraint on the whole AI trade, so data centers are migrating to where the power is, Texas and the Midwest, and the gas turbine market that was supposedly ebbing away to renewables has revived around 400 megawatt machines. Beyond the AI barbell, he argues the best industrial stories of his career are CEO-change margin stories, with 3M under Bill Brown the current case, and that the housing-levered names are the 2026 inflection trade once Fed easing gives visibility.
pushback: Eisman presses on why Eaton, traditionally a winner, lagged the electrical equipment trade, extracting that its class 8 truck businesses are down mid-teens and its automation business is flat, so it is not the pure AI play the market wanted. He sharpens the power argument into his own framing, that the stuff gets built by 2028 and the question is whether they can plug it in, which Coe adopts as exactly the binding constraint. He also runs the accountability segment, drawing out Coe's best and worst calls, including the GE underperform at 250 that became an upgrade near 90, and closes with the forcing question: if housing inflects in the second half of 2026, name the two stocks.
evidence: The ISM manufacturing index has been below 50 for 3 years and sits around 48
Eaton's two class 8 truck businesses are down roughly mid-teens this year while its automation business is flat
Large gas turbines put out about 400 megawatts each, and the market has revived after years of drift toward wind, solar and batteries
Coe put an underperform on GE at about 250 and upgraded it at about 90; he calls it his most impactful sell and now one of his better buys
About 70% of Lennox International's business is tied to residential housing, and about 80% of Stanley Black and Decker's sales are housing linked
Texas rationed electricity in the 2021 winter storm, a warning for the grid hyperscalers are counting on
shift: The two end aligned: the data center side of the barbell continues, it is too soon to buy consumer and housing exposure until the Fed easing path is visible, and the short cycle recovery is the big unresolved 2026 call. Eisman gets his specificity, Lennox and Stanley Black and Decker as the housing inflection names.
context: The interview that grounds the show's power-as-binding-constraint theme, a framing Eisman borrows from bank stress tests in his wraps, and it explains why GE Vernova is up over 100% in his year-end sector review. The housing discussion ties directly to the affordability theme of the December 5 wrap.

quotes.q: We've got pockets of growth, and then we've got a lot of no growth in the industrial sector right now.
They'll get this stuff built by 2028. The question basically is, can they plug it in?

questions: When does gas turbine supply actually catch up with data center power demand?
Will the ISM break back above 50 in 2026 and revive the short cycle industrials?
Does the housing inflection arrive in time for Lennox and Stanley Black and Decker, or is that a 2027 story?

title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part One) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 38
thesis: Part one of the lecture argues the crisis had four interlocking causes, too much leverage at systemic institutions, a large asset class that blew up, systemic ownership of that asset class, and derivatives tying balance sheets together, and then builds the first two from the ground up. Banks are unlike other businesses because ROE equals ROA times leverage: with a 1% return on assets a bank needs roughly ten times leverage to earn an adequate return, which is also its social purpose of recycling deposits into loans, so the question is never whether banks should be levered but how much is too much. Through the 2000s ROEs rose simply because leverage rose, and an entire generation of CEOs mistook leverage for genius. Meanwhile securitization removed the funding constraint on subprime lending, volume exploded from 20 billion in 1993 to about 600 billion by 2006 while underwriting collapsed, and when the buyer strike hit in summer 2007 refinancing stopped, loans repriced toward 9%, and the crisis became inevitable.
pushback: No guest challenges him, but he stress-tests his own story twice. First, he insists the anti-leverage moral is wrong as commonly told: we want banks levered so they can recycle deposits, like the porridge it has to be just right, so the failure was calibration and incentives, not leverage itself. Second, he flags the moment his short thesis wobbled, when March and April 2007 credit data improved, and explains why he held: tax refund season always flatters consumer credit, so the rally was an opportunity to add positions rather than a disconfirmation.
evidence: The key identity: ROE equals ROA times leverage, so a 1% ROA bank with no leverage earns a terrible 1% return on equity
The subprime industry generated only 20 billion in loans in 1993; by 2006 volume was around 600 billion a year, about 20% of the entire US mortgage market
The first pure subprime mortgage company went public in 1992, era names included the Money Store and Aames Financial
Borrow costs to short subprime stocks ran as high as 20% annually, which pushed his fund into shorting securitizations instead
Securitizations published 30, 60 and 90 day delinquency data every month, the disclosure that let him watch credit deteriorate in real time
When refinancing stopped in 2007, subprime loans repriced to a go-to rate of around 9% that borrowers could not afford
shift: As a lecture it moves toward a single claim: by late summer 2007, with the buyer strike in place, the financial crisis was already inevitable. He ends deliberately on that cliffhanger, deferring why inevitability became global collapse to part two.
context: The financial literacy masterclass strand at full length, formalizing the story he told live at Case Western weeks earlier. It also quietly underwrites his 2025 running argument on private credit: subprime was visible because securitizations disclosed monthly data, and private credit's danger is precisely that no such data exists.

quotes.q: An entire generation of bank CEOs mistook leverage for genius.
A bank sells you access to its balance sheet for a price.

questions: Where is the just-right leverage level between a bank too timid to serve its purpose and one that endangers the system?
Would monthly loan-level disclosure like subprime securitizations had make today's private credit risk visible?
What turned an inevitable subprime blowup into systemic collapse, the question part two exists to answer?

title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part Two) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 39
thesis: Part two completes the causal chain. Wall Street, paid entirely on volume, could not sell all the securitizations it was manufacturing, so it kept the excess AAA-rated paper on its own balance sheets, which is why the summer 2007 buyer strike doomed the system: the banks owned the asset class they had been selling, and incentives trump ethics every time. Credit default swaps, most of them written between systemically important firms, tied those balance sheets into a web nobody could map, so Lehman's failure and AIG's 80 billion of sold CDS turned a mortgage problem into a global one. Dodd-Frank then delevered and derisked the banks, creating the first real chief bank regulator, but with unforeseen consequences: compliance and technology costs made the big bigger, JPMorgan's deposit share going from 7.4% to over 12%. Silicon Valley Bank, he argues, was a liquidity and mark-to-market failure, not a capital failure, yet regulators fought the last war and demanded more capital, and the coming Trump-era changes, lighter stress tests and a friendlier vice chair, plus a bank merger wave, are the correction.
pushback: No outside voice pushes, but he confronts his own record and priors. The securitization heads he despised predicted they would buy back blown-up paper for pennies; he notes the irony that the prediction failed in reverse, since Wall Street never got the chance because it already owned the paper. More significantly, he announces a genuine reversal: after years of accepting regulatory hostility to bank M&A, he now believes the system needs many bank mergers so more banks can afford the technology arms race, and he says plainly that this is something he has changed his mind about.
evidence: AIG had sold about 80 billion dollars of credit default swaps when it hit trouble on September 16, 2008
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were seized on September 7, 2008, and Lehman went under on Sunday, September 14
Clayton Mortgage sampled roughly 10% of loan files, about 500 of the 5,000 mortgages in a typical 1 billion pool of 200,000 dollar loans
JPMorgan's deposit share has grown from 7.4% in 2008 to over 12% today, his exhibit for the big getting bigger
In 2022 the S&P fell 18% and Nasdaq 33% as rates rose, the shock that exposed Silicon Valley Bank's mark-to-market losses
By 2006 subprime origination of 600 billion a year produced more securitizations and CDOs than investors could absorb
shift: The lecture ends with a stated change of mind: Eisman, long comfortable with the post-crisis regime, now argues for a wave of bank mergers and predicts more lenient stress tests, better bank fundamentals and a friendlier regulator in Michelle Bowman replacing Michael Barr.
context: Closes the year and the financial literacy arc, and supplies the analytical spine for his weekly wrap positions: banks are safe because of post-2008 deleveraging, regulators repeat the last war, and the binding constraint metaphor he applies to AI power comes straight from the stress test regime described here.

quotes.q: Incentives trump ethics every time.
Generals always fight the last war.

questions: If stress tests become more lenient, does the system stay as safe as Eisman insists it now is?
Does a bank merger wave actually arrive, and would it fix the technology cost problem or just concentrate deposits further?
Would today's regulators catch a Silicon Valley style liquidity risk any faster than the 2023 ones did?

title: Steve Eisman Reacts to Scenes From The Big Short
thesis: Eisman's claim is that The Big Short compresses and invents on the surface while getting the mechanics and the emotion right underneath. The scenes he calls literary license, the taxi argument with his wife above all, never happened, but they encode a real condition, that shorting the entire housing market against unanimous opposition produced constant anxiety. The scenes he calls accurate are the technical ones, Lippmann teaching them how to short subprime paper, the dealers quoting credit default swap prices off screen, subprime bonds rising while defaults spiked. His conclusion is that the film's least flattering choice, the anger, was the most accurate, and he only accepted this after reading his own 2009 or 2010 testimony released in 2015.
pushback: No guest, so the pushback is against himself. His strongest self correction is on the portrayal: he told everyone the anger was overdone, then read his Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission transcript in the 2015 data dump and reversed on air. He also pushes back on the heroic framing of the trade by describing the Vegas trip as an attempt to find out that they were wrong.
evidence: The cast mapping, with Mark Baum as Eisman, Jared Vennett as Greg Lippmann of Deutsche Bank, and Vincent Daniel, Porter Collins and Danny Moses under their own names
Roughly 5,000 attendees at the January 2007 securitization conference at the Venetian, including hedge funds, rating agencies, banks and lenders
Morgan Stanley's internal hedge fund write-off in the fall of 2007 of at least 10 billion dollars, a full year before the general crisis
The Bear Stearns panel at Deutsche Bank held on the Friday it could not roll its paper, before the market opened, with the JP Morgan sale landing that Monday
The 2015 Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission document release, which made his own interview transcript publicly searchable
His one script contribution, changing a single insult to schmuck, which survived into the film with no credit
shift: Nothing shifts on the trade itself, which he has told many times. What moves is his account of himself. He arrives holding that Carell overplayed the anger and leaves holding the opposite, on the strength of a document rather than a memory.
context: The origin story the whole show runs on, and the source of the rules he applies to private credit and to AI capex in later episodes. The dealer quoted credit default swap price is his earliest version of the transparency complaint he now aims at private credit marks, and the Vegas trip is his template for going to meet the consensus before you bet against it.

quotes.q: Not only were we wrong, but everybody else was delusional.
Average people are going to be the ones that are going to have to pay for all of this.

questions: If dealer quoted pricing was the corruption he identified in 2007, where is the equivalent unobservable mark today?
What in the current market would play the role Morgan Stanley's 2007 write-off played, a single institution's loss that pre-announces the cycle?

title: 2026 Predictions with Dan Ives and Chris Verrone | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 40
thesis: Verrone's core argument is that one simple test survived a year of narrative whiplash: as long as bank stocks are working and credit is calm, the market trend is up, and both conditions held through deepseek in January, the tariff crash in April and every AI scare since, with 10-year yields remarkably stable underneath. Sentiment, not fundamentals, drove the swings, from euphoria in January to the second percentile at the April low, which is why the 37% rally off the bottom found so few believers. Ives layers on the tech case: it is still early in the AI trade, transformational names punish valuation-centric investors who trim on multiples, and even Apple has finally decided to play ball. Both expect 2026 up with white-knuckle moments, and the real work is sorting genuine AI winners from pretenders now that the label alone no longer carries a stock.
pushback: Eisman announces his pushback on the AI trade explicitly, using Eaton, unchanged since about April 2024, to show that a supposed AI darling with legacy businesses is not an AI play at all, and the panel concedes investors are now separating winners from what one guest calls the frauds, since saying AI 30 times on a conference call does not make you an AI play. On private credit he counters the bears: the canaries, First Brands and Tricolor, did not originate in private credit, and the negative case rests on a single number, growth from 2 trillion to 3 trillion, with no loss data behind it. He also insists his two 2026 risks, power timelines and the absence of a federal AI regulatory roadmap, are more serious than the panel's base case allows.
evidence: From February 19 through April 8, 2025 the market fell about 19 to 20% on tariffs, then rallied roughly 37% off the April low
Strategas's sentiment composite hit the second percentile historically around the April bottom
Private credit grew from 2 trillion in 2020 to 3 trillion today, the bears' main exhibit and, Eisman argues, their only one
Verrone calls Bank of America, a 55 dollar stock, conservatively worth 75 next year, with Wells Fargo, Goldman and Morgan Stanley already at new highs
Eaton has been roughly unchanged since April 2024 despite its AI halo, dragged by legacy truck and automation businesses
Verrone's added risk: a strong early-2026 economy pushes the 10-year back to 4.5% and triggers de-risking of speculative names
shift: Direction is never in dispute; the risk list is. Eisman signs on to the bull case except for his two named risks, energy and LLM law, Ives accepts the federal roadmap point, and Verrone appends a third risk, rates. Nobody concedes an AI bubble, and the argument ends as a ranking of what could break first.
context: The 2026 season opener, pairing the technician and the tech bull against Eisman's four 2025 themes from the year-end wrap. Verrone's banks-and-credit test is the market-facing twin of the Schorr private credit conversation, and the AI winners-versus-pretenders sorting picks up where the Nvidia and Burry depreciation debates in the November wraps left off.

quotes.q: So long as banks are involved and so long as credit is calm, the trend of the market's probably still up.
This is a 55 dollar stock today. I don't think it's a 55 dollar stock next year.

questions: Which cracks first in 2026: credit calm, power availability, or a 10-year yield back at 4.5%?
Can a federal AI regulatory roadmap arrive before a state-by-state patchwork chills the trade?
Does Bank of America reach Verrone's 75, and what would that confirm about the bank-led bull case?

title: The Broken US Healthcare System is Failing Millions of Americans with Warris Bokhari | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 41
thesis: Bokhari, a British-trained ICU doctor turned Anthem executive turned founder of Claimable, argues that all four pillars of American healthcare, commercial insurance, Medicare, Medicaid and the ACA, share one structural disease: the incentives reward denying care, because most patients never appeal even though appeals routinely succeed, sometimes in a day. Regulation entrenched the problem, barring providers from owning hospitals so they can only be bought, and fattening pharmacy benefit managers through rebates, while consolidation on both sides, Sutter Health style hospital monopolies and vertically integrated insurers, ratchets prices. Hospitals running 1.5 to 3.5% margins must treat everyone under EMTALA, so stripping coverage just shifts uninsured patients into emergency rooms the hospitals eat. He calls the whole drift defining deviancy down: denial of medically necessary care has become normal, and his answer is technology aimed at the denial chokepoint itself.
pushback: Eisman does not contest the thesis; he disciplines it. He forces the four-part taxonomy at the start, demands names and mechanisms throughout, who Sutter Health is, who David Joyner is, how a monopoly network negotiation actually works, and grounds every abstraction in a case: Bokhari's own inhaler prescription, taken since about 2007, denied by CVS the week before taping; the Austin breast surgeon Elizabeth Potter called out of surgery by UnitedHealth over a denial; the insurer's own employee whose denial was overturned in a day after her vision was already gone. The pressure is toward specificity rather than disagreement.
evidence: Most denied claims are never appealed, and appeals frequently succeed, some overturned within a single day
Hospital systems run at margins of roughly 1.5 to 3.5%, the difference between making and losing money
EMTALA, signed under Reagan in the 1980s, forces emergency rooms to treat regardless of insurance, and hospitals cannot balance-bill those patients
Sutter Health bought up regional California practices, promised no changes, then raised prices insurers could not refuse
Bokhari's own inhaler, prescribed continuously since about 2007, was denied by CVS the week before taping, prompting his letter to CEO David Joyner
Surgeon Elizabeth Potter was called out of an operation by UnitedHealth to be told her patient's coverage was effectively denied
shift: There is no adversary to move. Eisman, who opened by saying the episode exists because we are all human beings rather than stock pickers, closes calling the conversation great and very emotional, absorbing the argument that the failure is structural rather than a few bad actors. Bokhari ends on mission, his professor's eulogy, not on valuation.
context: The denials chapter of the show's running healthcare investigation, following Michael Ha's UnitedHealth work and framed by the Mangione trial happening blocks from the studio. It is also the clearest expression of the show's K-shaped economy theme at the human level, deliberately stripped of any stock angle.

quotes.q: We're going to talk about it not because we want to pick stocks, but because we're human beings.
He didn't try to make the world perfect. He just tried to make his corner of the world that little bit more perfect.

questions: Can automated appeals change insurer behavior, or will denial models simply adapt to the counterattack?
What regulatory change would actually break the provider consolidation ratchet Bokhari describes?
If the ACA is weakened, can hospitals at 3% margins survive the EMTALA load of newly uninsured patients?

title: Gary Marcus on the Massive Problems Facing AI & LLM Scaling | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 42
thesis: Marcus argues that large language models are statistical blur machines, not systems that build models of the world, and that this flaw is structural, not fixable by scale. Because they only predict which words cluster around other words in training data, they hallucinate constantly and break down on anything novel, from legal citations to bond market shocks to chess, where a model trained on the whole internet still makes illegal moves because it never abstracts the rules. He anticipated these failure modes in his 2001 book The Algebraic Mind, and GPT-5's underwhelming August 2025 debut, after repeated delays and a discarded intermediate model, is his proof that scaling has hit diminishing returns. The industry is therefore speculating hundreds of billions on the bet that a technology that does not work will magically work if made bigger, when what is needed is foundational research into systems that can induce causal world models. AI will transform the world eventually, just not with this technology and not on this timetable.
pushback: Eisman mostly plays prosecutor for the bull case, forcing Marcus to translate theory into market mechanics. He extracts the concession that each generation is legitimately better, just not enough better, and pushes the competitive logic to its end point: if the game is only scale, Google wins hands down because it makes its own tensor chips and can fund the commitments, while OpenAI next needs roughly a 100 billion dollar check that maybe five people in the world can write. Eisman also frames the novelty failure himself, asking whether the core problem is that anything not in the database breaks the model, which Marcus confirms is the central issue even for the newer inference models.
evidence: GPT-5 launched August 7, 2025, billed as able to do anything a PhD can do, and the public found the same hallucinations within about an hour
An earlier model internally treated as GPT-5 was demoted to GPT-4.5 because it was not good enough to carry the name
A tracker of fabricated legal citations in court filings found about 300 cases, then about 600 roughly three months later
Models trained on the entire internet, including the written rules of chess, still make illegal chess moves
Marcus wrote about hallucination and reasoning failures in The Algebraic Mind in 2001, and the transformer paper underlying LLMs dates to 2017
OpenAI's next funding round needs roughly a 100 billion dollar check, which maybe five people in the world can write
Ilya Sutskever, coming from the opposite camp, said in November that scaling alone is played out, converging with Marcus's five-year-old position
shift: No conversion, but a genuine update. Marcus holds his full position that scaling is an intellectual dead end, conceding only that models keep improving modestly. Eisman does not adopt the thesis on air; he calls the interview educational, tells wrap viewers that if Marcus is right the torrid growth in AI may slow with broad market implications, and immediately books Columbia's Daniel Guetta for a second opinion because the stakes are too high to rest on one critic.
context: This is the show's most direct examination of the foundation under its biggest running theme, AI capex and its returns: if Marcus is right, the 650 billion dollars of hyperscaler spending Eisman keeps tracking has no payoff. It pairs explicitly with the Daniel Guetta episode four weeks later, which Eisman commissions as the counter-opinion, and it feeds his lone wolf theme from the January 23 wrap, where Marcus sits alongside Michael Burry as a contrarian gaining traction.

quotes.q: Just making it bigger is not going to solve these problems. We need to do foundational research.
They never really abstract the model of how chess works. That's just so damning.

questions: If scaling is exhausted, what happens to the hundreds of billions of AI capex already committed for 2026?
Can OpenAI keep raising 100 billion dollar checks if Google wins a pure scale race?
How long would world-model research take to produce deployable systems, and who funds it in the meantime?

title: The Mystery of Stablecoins, Visa, & Fiserv’s Collapse with Ken Suchoski | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 43
thesis: Suchoski maps payments into three worlds: stablecoins, the newer players like PayPal, Block and Toast, and the old guard of Visa, Mastercard and the bank processors. His core argument is that stablecoins are real but narrow: their genuine value is 24/7 cross-border settlement with no cut-off times, attacking the correspondent banking system that still handles 90% of cross-border flows, yet the on and off ramps remain the choke point. Circle itself is best understood as an asset manager earning a reserve return that tracks short-term rates, so Fed cuts directly hurt it, which is why Autonomous was negative at an IPO valuation of about 75 times EBITDA. Across the rest of the group, a brutal year has left only Visa and Mastercard as durable long-term holdings, with everything else a trade whose main appeal is that beaten-down starting valuations mathematically improve prospective returns.
pushback: Eisman drives the risk questions rather than disputing conclusions. He flags what he calls potentially the biggest risk of the entire sector, what stands behind the peg, and walks Suchoski through the reserve mechanics until the rate sensitivity is explicit: the Fed cutting rates is a negative for Circle. He also forces the Fiserv autopsy, admitting he knew the stock had blown up but not why, and pushes on PayPal's premium pricing against Apple Pay, which Stripe passes to merchants for free. The episode ends with Eisman extracting a summing up and effectively co-signing it: Visa and Mastercard for the long term, the rest a minefield.
evidence: Circle traded at about 75 times EBITDA around its IPO, when Autonomous went negative on the stock
USDC reserves sit in very short duration assets, about a two week average duration in Treasuries
Specialist cross-border payment networks have about 10% of the cross-border market; correspondent banking still has the other 90%
The year's scoreboard: Fiserv down 71%, PayPal down 27%, Block down 30%, Bill down 36%, FIS down 17%, Toast down 2%, while Visa and Mastercard are up slightly
Only 2 of the 32 payment companies in Autonomous's screen outperformed the S&P 500
Merchant acquirers earn roughly 50 basis points on transactions; Cash App is about 60% of Block's gross profit and Square about 40%
shift: Convergence rather than conflict. Suchoski concedes the year was a minefield but holds that these remain high-return businesses whose lower valuations improve forward returns, and he stays optimistic. Eisman ends exactly where he started, with the position both men share: own Visa and Mastercard, treat everything else as a trade.
context: This is the show's crypto scepticism theme meeting real fundamental analysis: stablecoins get taken seriously as plumbing while Circle the stock gets dismantled on valuation and rate exposure. The Visa and Mastercard conclusion becomes a running Eisman rule he restates in the February wraps and again in the March 9 episode with Schorr and Collins, where stablecoin yield emerges as a threat to bank deposits.

quotes.q: Only two companies out of the 32 payment companies in our screen have outperformed the S&P 500.
It's like a minefield.

questions: Can stablecoins actually take share from the 90% of cross-border flows still in correspondent banking, given the on and off ramp problem?
What happens to Circle's earnings model in a sustained Fed cutting cycle?
Is Fiserv's 71% collapse a broken franchise or a mispriced processing annuity?

title: Jason Trennert on Populism, Policy & a Distorted Market System | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 44
thesis: Trennert argues that populism has dominated American politics for a decade because ordinary people got tired of social experiments from both left and right that never improved their lives, and that populism is now distorting the market system itself. Politically popular interventions, above all setting the price of money by pressuring the Fed, plus talk of policing buybacks and executive pay, replace market discipline with political discipline. Meanwhile the Fed has drifted from referee to active participant that shows up for every problem, Silicon Valley Bank included, and a government running large deficits as the reserve currency will eventually find the escape valve in higher inflation, a significantly weaker currency, or both. Near term he is constructive anyway: the One Big Beautiful Bill injects roughly 150 billion dollars of immediate refunds and stimulus plus supply-side provisions, so the 2026 economy should be pretty strong and the market should keep broadening beyond tech.
pushback: The two agree on fundamentals, so Eisman's pressure is Socratic rather than adversarial. When Trennert flips the SVB question back at him, Eisman answers flatly that he would have let it go down, never understanding why a bank that size was a big deal, sharpening Trennert's referee point. Eisman also presses on private equity marks, walking viewers through why the secondary market always clears at a discount, never at par, so a pension selling a stake marked at 100 is not getting out at 100. And he forces a midterm call from a self-described rock-ribbed Republican: if held today, Republicans lose the House.
evidence: Trennert, 57, was diagnosed with multiple myeloma two weeks before starting as Assistant Treasury Secretary for financial markets, spent about 3 weeks at Memorial Sloan Kettering, and now needs dialysis three times a week plus a donor kidney
The One Big Beautiful Bill should inject roughly 150 billion dollars of tax refunds and stimulus that gets spent right away
Private equity secondary market stakes always trade at a discount to par, never at 100
CME's prediction market deal with FanDuel went from five states to essentially 50 states in about 3 weeks
Polymarket, partnering with ICE, is a not insignificant Trump family holding
The UK's Liz Truss budget episode in the fall of 2022 stands as the template for a bond market disciplining a government
shift: No side moves because there is little distance to close: both hold that setting prices politically is corrosive, that the Fed should be a referee, and that prediction markets probably need regulation as the venue most ripe for insider trading. The one concession is political, Trennert admitting his own party likely loses the House. Eisman keeps his recession-free base case; Trennert keeps his strong 2026 call.
context: This episode threads the show's banks and Fed theme through a political lens, with Fed independence under literal criminal investigation pressure in the same period's wraps, and extends the private credit worry into private equity monetization and marks. The prediction markets riff also feeds Eisman's crypto scepticism: speculation migrating to FanDuel-style venues becomes the setup for George Noble's line three weeks later that Bitcoin is now for old people.

quotes.q: I don't think setting prices for anything is a good idea.
I can't think of anything that would be more ripe for insider trading than these markets.

questions: If the escape valve for deficits is inflation or a weaker dollar, what is the trigger and the timetable?
Does the One Big Beautiful Bill stimulus outrun the drag from tariff escalation in 2026?
Can prediction markets scale to 50 states without a regulator before an insider trading scandal forces one?

title: Consumer VibeCession & Private Credit Risk with Lakshmi Ganapathi | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 45
thesis: Ganapathi argues that the benign credit data in bank earnings is masking a deteriorating consumer, a disconnect she calls a vibecession. Invisible costs, health insurance, car repairs up roughly 45 to 50%, maintenance, have outrun wage growth, so households earning 100,000 to 150,000 dollars are cascading down into the lower leg of the K. The stress stays hidden because lenders are managing it out of the data: auto lenders extend and pretend, stretching a 3 year loan into 7 years or even a reported 100 month car loan, while BNPL spreads payments so thin that 19% of users simply forget obligations across Klarna, Affirm and PayPal. Lenders themselves do not believe the calm, quietly building near real-time consumer credit tracking and cutting limits at the point of sale. The cracks surface in the second half of 2026, showing up first as a pullback in consumer spending, not in credit statistics.
pushback: Eisman opens by stating the opposing evidence himself: bank numbers are fine, provisions flat, spending up, so she must reconcile her thesis with the data, which she does via the silent restructuring of loans. He then forces the falsification question, what pushes the consumer over the edge, and pins her to a timeline and a first canary. On stocks he exposes the limits of the short book: on Carvana she admits Unicus never looked at it because you do not short a cult, and on GE Vernova she concedes their short was run over as the stock mooned from about 250 to 700 on the AI power trade, leaving them sidelined.
evidence: Car repair costs are up roughly 45 to 50%, one of the invisible costs squeezing budgets
About 19% of BNPL users forget they have payments due because obligations are scattered across issuers, and rent and DoorDash can now be BNPL'd
A 100 month car loan on a depreciating asset has been reported as lenders extend terms to keep payments current
Consumers historically borrowed up to a 30% debt-to-income ratio; COVID-era originations ignored insurance, food and car maintenance costs
Michigan consumer sentiment sits at a multi-decade low while reported credit quality stays clean
Carvana went from about 4 dollars to over 400, a 100 bagger Unicus refused to touch
BNPL and card lenders are underwriting in near real time at the point of sale, declining customers without explanation
shift: Eisman buys the framing but not the timing as fact: he restates her case as the consumer being on the edge without yet being pushed over, and adopts deteriorating consumer spending as the first canary to watch. Ganapathi holds her second-half-2026 crack call and concedes nothing on it, while admitting the short side has no answer for cult stocks and AI moonshots.
context: This is the sharpest statement of the show's K-shaped economy theme, giving a mechanism for why the bottom of the K is invisible in bank data that Eisman praises weekly. Her closing points on private credit opacity, First Brands as the pattern where nobody knows until it is too late, feed directly into the Tom Gober and Schorr-Collins episodes in March, and Eisman quotes her getting in was easy line in his March 6 wrap.

quotes.q: No shorting the cult, no touching the cult.
Basically what you're saying is the consumer is on the edge, but hasn't been pushed over the edge.

questions: Does deteriorating consumer spending actually show up in the second half of 2026, or does extend-and-pretend keep working?
How much consumer risk has quietly migrated from banks into BNPL and private credit where nobody can see it?
If lenders are cutting limits in real time at the point of sale, does that itself trigger the spending downturn?

title: Daniel Guetta on the Guts of AI, Agentic AI & Why LLMs Hallucinate | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 46
thesis: Guetta, brought on as the explicit second opinion to Gary Marcus, agrees with Marcus's diagnosis but rejects his conclusion. Yes, LLMs are at bottom statistical parrots: they embed text into a space of numbers and predict what words sit nearby, which is exactly why they hallucinate and why they will not reach artificial general intelligence. But commercially that does not matter, because agentic AI, chatbots wired to tools that can book flights, send emails and act on systems, is already good enough to produce genuinely efficacious products. The binding constraint is not the model but the customer: companies must first build a fertile environment, IT systems a machine can actually operate, before AI pays off, and incumbents whose moat is control of a database are newly vulnerable.
pushback: The pushback runs through the episode's framing rather than combat: Eisman stages Guetta against Marcus and then adjudicates on air in a solo close. He tests the disruption logic with his own example, a hypothetical owner of the best commercial real estate database whose moat AI could now attack cheaply, and Guetta confirms the vulnerability. In his verdict Eisman raises the strongest objection himself: even if Guetta is right that products will work, nobody knows whether returns will justify the hundreds of billions being spent, and no answer is coming this year, only exciting announcements until 2027 or 2028.
evidence: The top four hyperscalers are set to spend about 650 billion dollars on AI-related capex

Guetta's route to the topic: a PhD in data-driven supply chain management with time at Amazon, years at Palantir's commercial business, then about 8 years building Columbia's data and analytics curriculum
Deep learning's breakthrough dates to the mid 2010s, with LLMs as one species of deep neural network defined by enormous parameter counts
Agentic AI announcements have already knocked around insurance brokers and wealth managers on single headlines
Eisman's timeline: whether the capex earns its return will not be knowable until 2027 or 2028
shift: Eisman moves, and says so: he sides a little more with Guetta than with Marcus, accepting that LLM products are good enough to matter even without AGI. What he refuses to concede to either side is the returns question, which he leaves explicitly open for two more years. Guetta gives ground to Marcus on hallucinations and AGI while holding that usefulness, not intelligence, is the investable fact.
context: The direct companion to the January 19 Gary Marcus episode and the clearest statement of where Eisman lands on the show's AI capex theme: spend continues, products arrive, verdict deferred. It also frames the AI panic mechanics of the February wraps, where software, brokers, logistics and real estate services stocks get shot on any agentic AI press release, the market pricing Guetta's thesis before the returns exist.

quotes.q: These models are just, at least right now, statistical parrots that are just parroting existing data.
We may not know till 2027, 2028 whether all this investment is going to produce returns that justify it.

questions: If products work but returns stay unprovable until 2027 or 2028, what keeps funding the 650 billion in the meantime?
Which database-moat businesses get attacked first now that the data, not the software, is the only barrier?
How many enterprises actually have the fertile IT environment agentic AI needs, and how long does building it take?

title: George Noble on Gold’s Rise, Crypto Doubts & Tesla’s Struggles | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 47
thesis: Noble's argument is R is for rotation, not recession: the market is not dying, it is changing leadership, so he is extremely negative on anything tech related and incredibly bullish on energy, materials, gold and silver. The gold case rests on fiat debasement, governments spending without constraint until a global Liz Truss moment when a bond market somewhere refuses the budget, as the gilt market did in the fall of 2022. Crypto fails its own test, digital gold that never hedges anything, its narrative machinery of four-year cycles and stock-to-flow just chart-and-story investing with no fundamentals. Tesla is the emblem of narrative over numbers: 2025 consensus earnings were 8 dollars three years ago and reality arrived around 1.70, on a stock that went nowhere for five years. Even the AI trade is underpriced product economics, ChatGPT-style teaser rates that must eventually rise, like Uber and DoorDash when free stock market money ran out.
pushback: Eisman engages Noble harder than most guests because they disagree on the core. On gold, Eisman is the open skeptic: as long as there is no alternative to Treasuries, he does not see the dollar getting flushed, and he notes people have made the debasement argument for 40 years while the US economy got a lot bigger along with the debt. He grants Noble's track record and stays open-minded on rotation without endorsing it. On Tesla he agrees with the analysis but not the trade, refusing to short anything that involves a cult. Only on crypto is there complete agreement.
evidence: Noble's Fidelity Overseas Fund was the country's number one fund in its first year, up 79% in 1985, and number two of all mutual funds over his six years
His 2008 fund was down only about 1% yet got redeemed heavily because it did not gate, becoming the ATM for investors
Tesla's 2025 consensus EPS three years in advance was 8 dollars; the actual number came in around 1.70, and the stock has gone nowhere in five years
The fall 2022 Liz Truss budget collapse in the UK gilt market is Noble's template for the coming global fiscal moment
An engineer contact pays 20 dollars a month for AI tools and sees no reason for the 200 dollar tier, and says the products are way underpriced for a decent return on equity
Young speculators have moved to FanDuel and prediction markets, leaving Bitcoin, in Noble's telling, to older holders
shift: Explicitly scored by Eisman in his close: open-minded but unconvinced on rotation into energy, a declared skeptic on gold and the dollar's demise, in complete agreement on crypto as speculation on speculation, and aligned on Tesla's fundamentals while refusing the short. Noble concedes nothing; both walk away holding their books.
context: The stock-jockey episode that stress-tests several show themes at once: crypto scepticism gets its sharpest line yet, the AI capex doubt gets a product-economics angle to complement Marcus's science and Burry's depreciation math, and the gold debate gives Eisman his cleanest statement of dollar confidence amid the silver mania chronicled in the surrounding wraps.

quotes.q: R is for rotation, not recession.
I generally do not like to short anything that involves a cult.

questions: What would force the global Liz Truss moment Noble expects, and which bond market breaks first?
If AI products must reprice from teaser rates to real economics, what happens to adoption and to the capex math?
Can the rotation into energy and materials persist if tech capex, the source of much demand, slows?

title: The Next Financial Crisis? Private Equity, Private Credit & Life Insurance | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 48
thesis: Gober, a forensic accountant and former state insurance examiner, argues that private equity's takeover of life insurance has quietly rebuilt the pre-crisis playbook. First, PE owners treat insurers as captive buyers of their own affiliated private credit paper, so asset risk is far higher than the plain vanilla bond books of old and the transactions are not at arm's length. Second, insurers cede liabilities to affiliated captive reinsurers, special purpose vehicles with no buildings and no employees, domiciled offshore or in five industry-friendly states that grant permitted practices exempting them from statutory accounting, which lets them hold fewer assets against the same promises. The result is hidden leverage nobody can measure, policed by fragmented state regulators who are outmatched by Apollo, KKR and Brookfield, and ignored by sell-side analysts who cover the parent asset managers but never read statutory filings. Policyholders and annuitants carry the tail risk.
pushback: Eisman does not resist the thesis, he stress-tests its remedies and its timing. When Gober offers his fix, make affiliated reinsurers file the same US statutory statements as domestic insurers, Eisman's response is good luck getting them to do that, because it would show they are not fully funded, and Gober agrees that is exactly why they will not. Eisman also supplies the reason nothing has blown up, a massive bull market in credit deferring problem one, and in his solo close he concedes the bear-case caveat that the risk is a slow boiling frog with no visible credit losses yet.
