evidence: Five states grant permitted practices that loosen statutory accounting: Vermont, South Carolina, Delaware, Arizona, Iowa
One company took reserve credit for 7 billion dollars laid off to three of its own captives, and when Gober saw inside such vehicles, assets were substantially short of liabilities
Gober has spent 41 years on insurer accounting since starting as a Mississippi examiner, including 7 years as an examiner passing twelve accreditation and certification exams
Reinsurance done properly requires sending assets commensurate with liabilities to an arm's length third party; only an affiliate would take 5 billion of liabilities with 3 billion of assets
Deferred acquisition cost treatment lets companies spread commissions already paid out over 25 years, underfunding future death claims
Athene recently ratcheted up its allocation to illiquid affiliated private credit investments significantly
shift: Eisman adopts the thesis wholesale and extends it. His close lays out four problems in his own words, captive purchases of affiliated paper, hidden offshore leverage, an analyst community not reading statutory filings, and lenient state regulation, and concludes the industry is a hell of a lot more leveraged than it looks, with regulators certain to act only after it blows up. Gober gives ground on nothing; the only open caveat, aired in the following wrap, is that no major credit losses have actually surfaced yet.
context: This is the show's private credit theme reaching its systemic endgame: the loans Lakshmi Ganapathi called opaque and Blue Owl gated now turn out to sit inside the vehicles backing life policies and annuities. The episode was pulled forward a week on Eisman's insistence, previews the Schorr and Collins discussion of the PE-insurer complex, and consciously echoes The Big Short structure, unregulated risk, captive structures, and regulators who move only after the explosion.

quotes.q: Just because the promise is somewhere else, it doesn't mean we no longer need to worry about our policy holders.
The only thing I can guarantee is that it's a hell of a lot more leveraged than it looks.

questions: What ends the credit bull market that is keeping the affiliated private credit books from being marked?
Could any state or federal actor compel captive reinsurers to disclose assets before a failure forces it?
If a PE-owned insurer fails, do state guaranty funds actually cover policyholders at today's scale?

title: Private Credit Cracks, The AI "Boogeyman" & Why Crypto is for Boomers | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 49
thesis: Schorr's core argument is that the panic in private credit stocks has run far ahead of the credit facts. Blue Owl and peers are down 30 to 50%, a BDC merger implying 80 cents on the dollar was cancelled after investors revolted, and retail is walking away, yet high yield spreads sit at all-time tights, bank CEOs report a healthy consumer, and direct lending deals typically carry roughly 75% equity beneath 25% debt, so a lot has to go wrong before lenders lose money. The stress is concentrated where five years of growth went, direct lending to software, while real estate credit, infrastructure debt and investment grade asset-backed finance are in decent shape. Collins adds the breadth: AI headlines are now repricing whole sectors on single press releases, bank M&A has disappointed the golden-age hopefuls, and stablecoins with yield workarounds are a real threat to the 29% of US deposits that pay zero interest.
pushback: Eisman's forcing question is the coexistence test, which Schorr poses with him: can private market stocks get pummeled while high yield spreads stay tighter than ever, every bank CEO calls the economy good, and every broker calls the capital markets cycle awesome? Something has to give, and neither guest fully resolves which side breaks. Eisman also makes them narrate the Blue Owl 80 cents fiasco in plain English, great news, we will give you 80 cents for your dollar, and pushes Collins on why bank M&A never became the tsunami with juicy premiums that he, too, had hoped for.
evidence: Private credit has grown to about 1.8 trillion dollars in total size
Blue Owl and similar stocks are down 30, 40, even 50% in 2026, and a merger that would have haircut fund investors about 20% was cancelled after bad press
Public BDCs were trading around 80 cents on the dollar as the merger was being pushed through
Direct lending buyouts are financed with roughly 75% equity and 25% debt, a thick cushion before the loans lose money
High yield spreads are at or near all-time tights even as private market stocks sell off
Insurance broker stocks fell about 10 to 12% in a day after OpenAI approved a Spanish AI insurance app on its platform
About 29% of US deposits pay zero interest, the pool yield-bearing stablecoins would attack
shift: Eisman comes away tentatively reassured on the credit itself, adopting Schorr's two anchors, tight spreads and the 75% equity cushion, as very interesting points against the panic, while leaving the coexistence paradox unresolved as the thing to watch. On payments the three converge on Eisman's old conclusion, Visa and Mastercard as the only long-term investments, everything else a trade. Schorr holds that real losses have not appeared and investors are de-risking ahead of evidence.
context: The calm-side rebuttal in the show's private credit arc, landing one week after Tom Gober's alarm about PE-owned insurers and a month after Blue Owl froze redemptions: Eisman deliberately alternates the prosecution and the defense. It also stitches together the AI headline-risk mechanics from the February wraps and the stablecoin deposit threat first raised with Ken Suchoski, tying private credit, AI fear and payments into one financial sector picture.

quotes.q: Can all those things coexist? Can that really happen?
The only long-term investments in payments these days is Visa and Mastercard. Everything else is just a trade.

questions: Which breaks first: all-time tight high yield spreads or the pummeled private market stocks?
If retail keeps walking away from direct lending funds before losses appear, does the redemption pressure itself create the losses?
Does software disruption ever burn through the 75% equity cushion in direct lending deals?

title: The Iran War Crisis: Ex-CIA Analyst Helima Croft on Oil Shock & Energy Risk | The Weekly Wrap
thesis: Croft argues the administration underpriced the risk of the Iran war because it anchored on two recent templates: Venezuela, where installing Delcy Rodriguez showed goals could stay manageable without full regime change, and the June 12-day war, where markets faded the story once no supply disruption materialized. This war is different because energy infrastructure does not restart like a light switch: Saudi Arabia's best-in-class Aramco could resume quickly, but Iraq's degraded infrastructure means a long restart, and LNG liquefaction facilities take even longer once cooled down and shut. If the strait stays closed, storage hits tank tops and the market breaks again, with the Saudi East-West pipeline to the Red Sea the main comfort. Her deepest warning is her own admitted bias from Iraq: enlightened interventions go wrong through mission creep, because the adversary gets a vote and will try to raise costs high enough that America never comes back.
pushback: Eisman plays interrogator on mechanics rather than adversary: he forces her to explain exactly why restarting liquefaction is not a light switch, makes her trace the East-West pipeline country by country to the Red Sea, and pulls out her CIA background for the audience. When she names Iraq as her formative bias, he sharpens it into the direct question of whether the same failure to prepare for the day after could repeat here, which she accepts.
evidence: Oil breached the $100 level on Monday and collapsed in real time as Trump told CBS News the war would be over soon
Croft walked into the CIA on December 1, 2001, at the start of her career
The June 12-day war between Israel, Iran and the US produced only a brief oil run-up before markets faded the story
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline lets it export from the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz
Iraq's infrastructure and investment problems mean a much longer production restart than Aramco's
If the strait stays closed long enough, oil storage hits tank tops and the market starts breaking again
shift: No clash to resolve: Eisman absorbs Croft's framework and calls the interview one of the most informative he has run. Croft holds her caution that the administration's Venezuela and June templates may not fit, and Eisman adopts her mission-creep warning as the thing to watch.
context: This is the episode where the show pivots from the K-shaped economy and private credit to a war-driven unipolar market, with Eisman declaring that geopolitical uncertainty has overwhelmed all traditional equity analysis. It launches the Iran arc that continues with Steven Cook on March 30 and John Spencer on April 14, and it is also the episode where Eisman retires the chemotherapy hat, bought at The Gap.

quotes.q: You start with one set of objectives, and those objectives change. And then you get caught, because your adversary has a say.
The level of uncertainty that is created overwhelms any traditional equity analytical tools.

questions: How long can the Strait of Hormuz stay closed before storage tank tops force a genuine supply break?
Does the administration's Venezuela template survive an adversary determined to raise the cost of ever coming back?
If restart timelines differ this much by country, who supplies the marginal barrel when the war ends?

title: Mark Cuban Shares His Plan For Fixing Drug Prices in America | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 50
thesis: Cuban argues American drug prices are high not because drugs cost too much to make but because the delivery system is built on perverse incentives. Pharmacy benefit managers, which exist only in the US, collect rebates from pharma companies that function as bribes for placement on preferred formularies, and those rebates get pocketed rather than passed to consumers, while the so-called wholesale acquisition cost is actually the retail price people pay. The PBMs are owned by the giant insurers, an oligopoly with thousands of subsidiaries that can shift profit between pockets and game medical loss ratios. Meanwhile, deductibles many Americans cannot afford mean they effectively have no insurance, turning doctors and hospitals into subprime lenders who extend care they will never be paid for. Cost Plus attacks all of it with one published price for everyone: cost plus a 15% markup.
pushback: Eisman keeps forcing the who-actually-pays question: if a drug wholesales for a thousand and the rebate is 400, is the consumer paying a thousand, 600, or something in between? That extracts Cuban's cleanest structural point, that in pharmacy the wholesale price equals the retail price. Eisman also presses on whether anyone has copied the model (no one has, though companies borrow his published contracts) and draws out the claim that insurers threatened to cut off pharma companies that worked with Cost Plus.
evidence: Cost Plus sells prescription drugs at cost plus a 15% markup, one published price for everyone
PBMs exist only in the United States, and the largest insurers own them
In the example discussed, a drug wholesaling for 1,000 dollars carries a rebate of about 400 that the consumer rarely sees
The biggest insurance company has 2,600 subsidiaries, enabling left pocket, right pocket intercompany transfers that distort medical loss ratios
A 1,500 dollar deductible counts as low, yet many Americans cannot afford it, which means they effectively have no insurance
Cuban's own employee health plan uses no insurance company at all and has zero out-of-pocket costs for employees
Cuban says he made 80% plus a year trading tech stocks in the 1990s but is now mostly in cash, in the Warren Buffett camp
shift: Eisman is fully persuaded: his closing monologue adopts Cuban's framework wholesale, calling rebates bribes and PBMs a hidden scheme, and ends hoping Cuban succeeds. The surprise concession runs the other way on markets, where Cuban reveals he is largely in cash waiting for the tide to go out.
context: The third installment of the healthcare investigation, after Michael Ha on insurance economics in September and Waris Bokhari on claim denials in January, and it feeds directly into Ha's return one week later. It also reinforces two running Eisman rules: opacity is itself a sell signal, and misaligned incentives, not costs, are what break American healthcare.

quotes.q: In pharmacy, the wholesale price is the retail price.
Essentially, pharma companies bribe PBMs to get on those formularies via the rebates.

questions: Can one transparent price list actually force an oligopoly of insurer-owned PBMs to reprice?
Why has no one copied Cost Plus after years of published prices and contracts?
If providers are the new subprime lenders, who eventually eats the losses they are quietly accruing?

title: The Only Health Insurance Stock You Can Own with Michael Ha | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 51
thesis: Ha argues managed care is being hit by a one-two punch across every business line at once. Risk adjustment crackdowns are squeezing the coding gains that inflated Medicare Advantage revenue, while rate notices came in flat when everyone expected roughly 5%, repeating the margin deterioration and benefit cuts of 2024 and 2025 and now threatening 2027. Medicaid is broken separately: redeterminations dropped the healthy members, leaving a sicker pool whose rates will take up to 24 to 36 months to reprice actuarially, which is the real answer to when to buy Molina. The deepest problem is structural: the industry became vertically integrated through acquisitions rather than organically, so companies with thousands of subsidiaries and databases that do not talk to each other are vertically integrated without being integrated, which is why an oligopoly cannot extract even normal rent.
pushback: Eisman forces the macro how question: vertically integrated oligopolies are supposed to extract excess rent, so why is this industry a disaster? Ha's answer, that the integration came by acquisition and never operationally happened, becomes Eisman's headline takeaway. Eisman also translates Ha's Medicaid actuarial walk into the blunt investor question, we are basically asking when do I buy Molina, and pins him to the 24 to 36 month answer.
evidence: Medicare Advantage rate notices came in flat against a consensus expectation of about a 5% increase
Medicaid rates take up to 24 to 36 months to reflect today's sicker acuity mix after redeterminations
Risk scores are multipliers on a benchmark: the average is 1.0, but comorbidities can push a member to 2.0, 3.0 or 5.0
The largest insurer has 2,600 subsidiaries whose technology databases do not speak to one another
Ha estimates the tail risk of Congress breaking these companies up has moved from maybe 1% to 5 or 10%
European investors Ha visited were sitting on hundreds of millions, if not billions, of unrealized losses in the sector
shift: Eisman ends more bearish than he began: too early to buy the sector, expect it to keep doing terribly. Ha holds that managed care remains a good long-term space if you are very selective, singling out ALHC as the one name he loves, which Eisman admits he has not yet examined.
context: The fourth healthcare episode and Ha's return after his September UnitedHealth breakdown, taped one week after Mark Cuban made the PBM case from the outside; Ha confirms from the inside that PBMs have fee-based levers to survive rebate reform. The vertical-integration-without-integration insight becomes a recurring Eisman explanation for why scale has failed this industry.

quotes.q: While they are vertically integrated, they're not integrated.
If the tail risk was 1% before, it might be 5% or 10% now, which you should really risk weight.

questions: Does Medicaid pricing actually catch up in 24 to 36 months, or do states cut the timeline first?
Can any acquirer-built insurer genuinely integrate 2,600 subsidiaries, and what would that cost?
If flat rates repeat for 2027, which seniors' benefits get cut next and who wears the political blame?

title: The Iran War is Masking Economic Problems: Why Housing is So Expensive | The Weekly Wrap
thesis: Lord, CEO of Meritage Homes, argues housing is expensive because the country is structurally underbuilt: after the Great Recession builders pulled back, lots never came to market, and pent-up demand then collided with the last five years of shocks. The affordability crisis is concentrated below the median, so Meritage deliberately builds product under half a million dollars nationwide, the price point where people are actually struggling to attain ownership, while the median US home now costs more than that. On strategy, he defends a land-light model: bringing land on the books only when ready to build homes maximizes working capital efficiency and returns, but he concedes the off-balance-sheet route is not free, since competitors using REIT mechanisms pay for it in margin. It is all math, trading IRR impact against capital efficiency.
pushback: Eisman pushes on the valuation hierarchy: why do Lennar, DHI and Pulte earn higher ROEs and price-to-book multiples while Meritage and other roughly 5 billion dollar builders trade near tangible book, which is exactly why he recommended the stock. On land banking he forces the concession that off-book land costs margin, summarizing Lord's answer as no free lunch here, which Lord accepts before reframing it as a capital efficiency trade worth making.
evidence: The median home price in the US is over half a million dollars, and Meritage targets product below that line
Meritage's market cap is around 5 billion dollars versus roughly 20 billion for Lennar and up to 45 billion for DHI
Eisman recommended MTH earlier in the year when it traded at tangible book value
The US has been underbuilt since the Great Recession as builders backed off bringing lots and supply to market
Private builders had a captive audience of shoppers until roughly the middle of last year
Competitors using a REIT land mechanism carry an incremental margin burden for keeping land off the books
shift: Neither side moves much: Eisman sticks with his Meritage recommendation and his tangible book framework, and Lord concedes the margin cost of land-light strategies while holding that capital efficiency wins the trade. The interview hardens Eisman's view that midsize builders below tangible book are the right way to own the affordability story.
context: The housing affordability thread made flesh: Eisman has argued for months that homes are unaffordable for the bottom of the K-shaped economy, and here the builder confirms the structural undersupply diagnosis. The episode pairs with the January MTH recommendation and the April earnings wraps, where Meritage prints 82 cents against a 51% decline and Eisman restates the long-term tangible book case.

quotes.q: We really underbuilt in this country.
No free lunch here is basically what you're saying.

questions: How long can builders profitably serve the under half a million segment if land and rate costs keep rising?
Does the land-light model's margin cost show up as a disadvantage when the cycle turns down?
What closes the ROE gap between the big three builders and the 5 billion dollar tier: scale, land strategy, or just time?

title: Inside the Iran War with Steven Cook: What’s REALLY Happening? | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 52
thesis: Cook argues the war is genuinely hard to read because information streams are corrupted, but the asymmetry of aims is legible: Israel's objectives are clear, regime change, the missile program, the nuclear program and the proxies, while Trump has deliberately left US aims vague to preserve deal-making maneuverability. The regime has proven far more resilient than expected even with degraded command and control, because at every escalation the Iranians have had an answer, and closing the strait does not take much. His base case is messy: the regime survives, Gulf states arm up, the strait may or may not reopen, and victory stays unclear, though the Iranian people are yet to be heard from and revolutions unfold over many months. Any negotiated end requires verifiable limits on restarting the nuclear program, or the whole war will have been for naught.
pushback: Eisman's sharpest press comes on the highly enriched uranium: when Cook relays the Israeli view that the Iranians cannot get at it, Eisman objects that it is sitting in their own country, forcing Cook to explain that the sites are so devastated the material is buried and any recovery attempt would be seen. He also makes Cook drop the analyst's hedge twice, first asking what goals Cook would set if he were in the room, drawing out the JCPOA-style answer, and then demanding a bet on what the Middle East looks like in a few months.
evidence: Recorded March 23, the day Trump announced a 5-day pause on bombing oil infrastructure that Iran promptly denied negotiating
Trump said 4 to 6 weeks; the war is in its fourth week with energy prices elevated and questions mounting
The upward estimate is 30,000 civilians killed by their own government in the December to January crackdown
The Iranian revolution unfolded over roughly 15 to 18 months, Cook's caution against expecting instant uprisings
After the Abraham Accords, Trump ordered Israel into CENTCOM, obliging even hostile neighbors like Qatar to work with it
Some 18 foreign ministers gathered in Saudi Arabia last week and issued statements far tougher on Iran than on Israel
Iran fired on Dimona after the Natanz strikes and missed by about 12 miles
shift: Eisman concedes ground: he hopes for a clear victory but accepts Cook's messy base case as the likelier world, closing that if things are messy, the markets will just have to deal with it. Cook holds his structural pessimism while granting the damage to Iran's missile and nuclear programs is real.
context: The second leg of the Iran arc after Helima Croft's oil-shock framework, and the scholarly counterweight to John Spencer's more bullish military read two weeks later. It feeds Eisman's running market rule for this stretch: a unipolar, headline-trading market where war aims kept deliberately vague translate directly into unpriceable uncertainty.

quotes.q: Otherwise, this will be all for naught.
He's a deal guy and he wants as much maneuverability as possible.

questions: Can any ceasefire include verification strong enough to prevent a nuclear restart?
Does the regime's survival plus an armed-up Gulf produce stability or just a paused war?
When, if ever, do the Iranian people move, given the revolution's 15 to 18 month precedent?

title: Is Private Credit the Next Systemic Crisis? Steve Liesman Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 53
thesis: Liesman argues the economy faces four simultaneously consequential stories, tariffs, AI job losses, private credit and the oil shock, any one of which would normally be enough, and the only honest method is scenario analysis because short, medium and long wars produce dramatically different outcomes. Against the gloom he sets the unforecastable resilience of a segmented US economy that contains an oil economy the size of Saudi Arabia inside it. On private credit his two key insights are that the equity private equity puts into buyouts may itself be borrowed from banks, so true leverage is unknowable, and that opacity itself is the panic mechanism: if losses were small but everyone knew who held them, nobody would be scared. On the Fed, hawks are floating policy action to keep inflation expectations anchored against the oil spike, while Powell stands pat.
pushback: The sharpest disagreement is over the hawks: when Liesman reports Kansas City-style voices suggesting policy action against oil-driven inflation, Eisman objects that raising rates to fight an exogenous event makes little sense, and Liesman largely agrees. Liesman also plays devil's advocate on private credit, relaying the software industry's counter-story to Eisman's relentless weekly bad-news drumbeat, and reframing private credit's 2 to 1 leverage as conservative next to banks at 12 to 1, perhaps proof that Dodd-Frank pushed lending out of banks too far.
evidence: Recorded after 4 pm on March 31, following an enormous rally on a Wall Street Journal report that Trump would end the war without reopening Hormuz
About 80% of direct lending finances private equity buyouts, an incestuous loop since PE firms own the credit funds
Roughly 25% of direct lending is estimated to sit in software companies bought out between 2018 and 2022
Banks are levered about 12 to 1 versus private credit funds at roughly 2 to 1
The US oil economy is about the size of Saudi Arabia's entire economy
Bank of America's internal consumer data shows the lower-end consumer, who did well during COVID, is now clearly hurting
shift: Eisman comes away with two insights he admits he did not have: buyout equity may itself be levered, and opacity rather than size is what drives the panic. Both hold their base positions, Eisman that a credit cycle is coming through software, Liesman that scenario uncertainty and the economy's resilience make confident forecasts impossible.
context: This episode fuses three of the show's running threads: the war-driven unipolar market, the private credit investigation, and the K-shaped economy, with the Bank of America low-end consumer data extending the affordability theme. Liesman's opacity point becomes a fixture of Eisman's wraps, where he argues nobody knowing who holds the risk is itself the systemic problem.

quotes.q: If all I had to do was figure out the effects of a surge in oil prices on the economy, that would be enough.
We have an oil economy the size of Saudi Arabia inside the US economy.

questions: How much hidden leverage sits beneath private equity's supposedly unlevered buyout equity?
Would disclosure alone, knowing who holds what, defuse the private credit panic without any losses being taken?
Can the Fed hold inflation expectations anchored through an oil shock without raising rates into a war?

title: Catching a Falling Knife: The Truth About Software Stocks Today | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 54
thesis: Oliver argues software's decades of outperformance rested on systems of record: businesses outsourced what they did not want to build, the resulting platforms became sticky because change management is painful, and stickiness meant pricing power through every platform transition. AI attacks the foundation, because anyone can now create software in minutes, which is simultaneously a golden age of creation and a threat to the moats, seat counts and per-seat pricing that anchor every software model. His key defense is that nothing has actually happened yet: contacts among buyers and companies report no changed behavior, and the group's collapse is investors fighting an unprovable negative. Clarity requires three to four quarters of pattern-forming anecdotes on retention and upsell, and innovative incumbents with proprietary data should make it through to the other side.
pushback: Eisman grants the survival case but presses the pricing point: even if Salesforce is still great in two or three years, revenue growth must slow because pricing power cannot survive a collapse in the cost of creating software, and until he knows how much lower estimates go, he will not touch the group. He also tests the proprietary database thesis, that a Moody's or S&P selling data plus software is the best position, and detours into disclosure, marveling that only one company in Oliver's entire coverage reports GAAP numbers.
evidence: Software valuations have been cut by more than half, and the group trades at a huge discount to the S&P for roughly the first time ever
The whole revenue model reduces to two variables: growth in seats times average price per seat, and both are now at risk
Only one company in Oliver's coverage universe reports GAAP earnings
Web content creation is exploding, visible in domain creation data and traffic at companies like Cloudflare
The iPhone analogy: it took multiple years after launch before it killed the yellow cab, so AI's damage may arrive slowly
Oliver expects three to four quarters before public investors can see whether buyer behavior actually changes
shift: Nothing converges: Oliver stays constructively optimistic that innovative incumbents cross the tunnel, while Eisman closes that the tunnel's end is at least a year away and buying now is catching a falling knife. Eisman's one concession is that cheapness itself is meaningless here, since software investors read low valuation as a symptom, not an opportunity.
context: This episode gives the fundamental engine behind the private credit story the show has tracked for months, since roughly 25% of direct lending sits in bought-out software companies, and it frames the AI capex debate from the demand side: AI as a destroyer of existing software economics rather than a boon. It sets up the April wraps on internalization and the Apollo interview two weeks later.

quotes.q: Nobody loves software right now.
Trying to buy the group here is like catching a falling knife.

questions: Can per-seat pricing survive when the marginal cost of creating software approaches zero?
Which anecdotes, retention, upsell, internalization, would count as the pattern that ends the uncertainty?
If proprietary data is the real moat, how many software companies actually have one?

title: John Spencer on What the Headlines Get Wrong About the Iran War | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 55
thesis: Spencer argues the contradictory headlines miss that the US and Israel have systematically degraded Iran's military: the missile program, the nuclear program, the navy, and the internal suppression apparatus like the Basij, using technology, deception and intelligence penetration that did not exist a generation ago. Regime change is not the goal, only a nice-to-have; the four real goals, ending nuclear capability, ballistic missiles, and power export while changing regime behavior, are all achievable, and Iran's lashing out at its neighbors has validated the operation's necessity to every Gulf state. The larger stake is demonstrative: the US has staged an unprecedented show of military prowess, and Russia and China, whose untested equipment just failed by proxy, are taking notes, which should make Xi rethink Taiwan. On the other side of the war he expects more stability, not less.
pushback: Eisman confronts him with the opposite narrative directly, citing the Foreign Policy editor-in-chief's headline that Trump is losing the war, and asks what Iran has actually accomplished with its missiles and the closed strait; Spencer answers that Iran has mostly validated the case against itself. Eisman also plays the useful novice, forcing concrete details, where the B-2s flew from, how long the missions ran, how the pilot rescue worked, that turn Spencer's argument from assertion into mechanics.
evidence: The war is in its fifth week at recording, the day of Trump's press conference on the rescued pilot
B-2 bombers flew from Missouri, roughly 18 hours each way, to strike Iran
The deception plan sent seven B-2s toward the Middle East and six toward Guam as a feint
Twenty years ago an entire corps of about 20,000 soldiers attacking Baghdad had exactly one drone
The supreme leader was reportedly tracked partly by tapping Tehran's highway cameras as sensors
The pilot rescue succeeded without a single death or injury
shift: Eisman buys the core claims: the degradation of Iran's military is unquestionable, the Taiwan implication is the sleeper insight, and postwar stability would be very positive for markets. He does not fully adopt Spencer's optimism on timing, noting the only open question is how long achieving the goals takes.
context: The third and most bullish leg of the Iran arc, balancing Steven Cook's messy base case from two weeks earlier and completing the show's escalation from Croft's oil mechanics to grand strategy. For the market thread, it feeds Eisman's view that the war is the single variable and that a decisive, stabilizing outcome is the underpriced scenario.

quotes.q: As Sun Tzu said, deception is everything in a war.

questions: How long can achieving the four goals take before market patience and coalition cohesion crack?
Does China actually update on Taiwan, or does it read Iran as a poor proxy for its own military?
Can regime behavior change be verified without the regime change Spencer says is not the goal?

title: Market Patterns Work and Jeffrey Hirsch Explains Why | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 56
thesis: Hirsch argues market seasonality persists because stocks are bought by people, people run on psychology, and even the algorithms are written by people, so patterns like the midterm election cycle, the January barometer and the best six months keep working across decades. The discipline is in the method: seasonality is never used alone but confirmed with a momentum tool like MACD before entry or exit, and patterns must be tracked honestly and retired to the indicator graveyard when they die, as the September reverse barometer did. His father Yale's rules anchor the book: write down your losers, because if you do not profit from your investment mistakes, somebody else will. Newer wrinkles include a 5-year Trump-era cycle of Q1 shocks negotiated away through year-end.
pushback: The liveliest friction is over Bitcoin, where the skepticism is mutual: Hirsch complains he cannot even define a close for an asset trading 24/7 across venues, and Eisman answers that Bitcoin acts opposite to its thesis, trading like 2x to 4x the Nasdaq, so just buy a levered Nasdaq ETF instead. Eisman also probes for falsification, asking which patterns stopped working, and gets the graveyard answer rather than a defense of everything, while Hirsch dismisses black swan forecasting outright: if you could foresee them, you would not need the book.
evidence: Yale Hirsch started the Stock Trader's Almanac in 1966, and the book is now in its 60th year of annual editions
The midterm-year pattern: volatility bottoms around September and October, then the market rallies through April of the following year
The January barometer: when the market rises in January, the year is up more often than not
The September reverse barometer stopped working and was retired to the indicator graveyard
Since 2008, working with technician David Aronson, the Almanac has used MACD to confirm best six months entries and exits
Bitcoin trades like roughly 2x to 4x the Nasdaq, and its old seasonal patterns no longer work
shift: No real contest: Eisman endorses the book outright and adopts its core premise that human psychology creates durable patterns, algorithms included. The shared conclusion is methodological, that patterns earn trust only while they keep working and must be buried when they stop.
context: An evergreen entry that still lands on two running themes: the crypto skepticism thread, with both men dismissing Bitcoin as a levered Nasdaq proxy without a definable close, and the war backdrop, where Hirsch's taco trade cycle of Q1 shocks maps onto the March to April double bottom. It is the show's lightest episode in a stretch dominated by Iran and private credit.

quotes.q: If you don't profit from your investment mistakes, somebody else will.
Who creates the algorithms? People.

questions: How would you know in real time that a 60-year pattern has died rather than paused?
Does the midterm bottom pattern survive a market where a single war headline swamps seasonality?
If algorithms increasingly trade against known seasonals, do the patterns arbitrage themselves away?

title: Apollo's Private Credit Exposure: Chris Edson Weighs In | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 57
thesis: Edson argues the private credit panic conflates the industry's riskiest corners with lenders built nothing like them. Apollo is primarily a diversified originator, 16 lending platforms with 4,000 employees spanning fleet, aircraft lending and more, funding the real economy the way insurance capital has for a century, and CFOs come to it to de-risk multibillion dollar capex borrowing after years of market shocks. Its software exposure is small by design, because Apollo underwrites value and collateral and software offers neither, being a dollar and a dream. On alignment and liquidity, the two live controversies, he argues Apollo is structurally different: it owns Athene and holds 35 billion dollars of its own capital as first loss, less than 5% of its capital sits in redeemable retail vehicles, and Athene's regulatory filings list every single loan, rebutting the opacity charge.
pushback: Eisman raises the traditional principal-agent question directly and lets Edson answer with the Athene first-loss structure, then presses on the redemption gate scandal, extracting the contrast that under 5% of Apollo's capital is redeemable while peers like Blue Owl carry much higher exposure, with Edson conceding the industry must honor what is fair. Eisman also pushes the software question until Edson, while declining to bad-mouth competitors, admits the range of outcomes is wide and companies with no moat, no proprietary data and quick installation are genuinely at risk.
evidence: Apollo runs 16 origination platforms with about 4,000 employees
Apollo holds 35 billion dollars of its own capital in Athene as the first-loss position
Less than 5% of Apollo's capital is redeemable on a regular basis, versus much higher percentages at firms like Blue Owl
Fleet leasing serves the largest corporates running 10 to 20,000 vehicles, and PK Air Finance was bought out of GE Capital
Edson built a Junie B. Jones math game for his 8-year-old with AI in seconds, his own exhibit for why software moats are in question
Athene's regulatory filings list every loan it holds, with counterparty and amount
shift: Eisman concedes the specific while keeping the general: Apollo's software exposure looks genuinely small and its alignment and disclosure claims check out, but his conclusion is unchanged, a credit cycle is coming and it will run through software. Edson never disputes that software has major AI-driven issues, only that Apollo is standing where the flood will hit.
context: The defense's turn in the months-long private credit investigation, after weeks of wraps cataloguing redemption gates, frauds and software exposure, and two weeks after Rob Oliver supplied the AI-versus-software mechanics. It sharpens the show's emerging distinction between collateral-based lending and the direct lending funds levered to bought-out software, the same split Eisman uses when parsing Ares and Blue Owl in the wraps.

quotes.q: We own Athene. We're the first loss in Athene.
A credit cycle is coming. It's going to be there in software.

questions: If Apollo sidesteps the software bust, which lenders are actually holding the concentrated exposure?
Does listing every loan in insurance filings amount to real transparency if nobody reads them until trouble hits?
Can quarterly redemption vehicles survive a real credit cycle, or are gates now a permanent feature?

title: Is a Market Melt-Up Coming? Why Tech & Semis Are Dominating Again | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 58
thesis: Verrone and Sohn argue that price action, not headlines, is telling the truth about this market. The 2026 war swoon, with the Nasdaq down 7% and the S&P down 4% into a March 31 low, is a near replay of 2025's tariff swoon from late February to April 9, and in both cases the market snapped back to new highs faster than anyone reading the news would have predicted. What matters most is that leadership came right back to the same names, AI and power stocks, semis, industrials and banks, which by their work confirms the trend rather than ending it. Because leadership reasserted so quickly, Verrone raises his odds of a 1999-style melt-up over the next several months. Sohn's caveat is structural: semis are now so large inside the S&P 500 that passive investors own far more of the story than they realize, so the prudent move is to diversify into energy, materials and alternatives before the story hits a speed bump.
pushback: Eisman does not fight the bullish read so much as stress test its edges. He forces them to explain gold, which should have soared when war broke out and instead went nowhere, and Verrone concedes gold jumped the shark from safe haven to risk asset back in the October to January runup. Eisman also injects his own fundamental jab on the banks, mocking Wells Fargo for a culture of blowing a quarter like clockwork after its net interest margin fell 13 basis points sequentially, and he presses on whether any defensive group can lead, which Sohn answers in the negative: staples outperformed for two weeks and gave it all back.
evidence: At the March 31 low the Nasdaq was down 7% and the S&P down 4% for the year; both are now up, with the S&P at new highs
Semis are now about 17% of the S&P 500, roughly half of the entire tech sector weight
Software has shrunk from the teens to single digits as a share of the index
Wells Fargo's net interest margin fell 13 basis points sequentially, a massive move for a bank
GE reported orders up roughly 80%, which Verrone cites as a non-recession indicator even as street economists raised recession odds in March
Gold underperformed throughout the war episode after a blow-off condition in January
Consumer staples outperformed for only 2 weeks during the swoon before giving it all back
shift: Eisman ends up adopting the deja vu framing wholesale in his closing thoughts, and says he is thinking about increasing energy exposure, not cutting it, because the group is oversold in a long-term uptrend. Verrone holds his melt-up call, Sohn holds his diversification warning about semi concentration, and no one aired a bear case beyond getting too static in one's views.
context: This episode sets the market backdrop for the whole late spring run of the show: the war swoon and recovery that the weekly wraps keep referencing, and the semi concentration that the Rasgon episode in June treats as the center of the universe. Eisman's melt-up nervousness shows up a week later in the May 15 wrap title, and the banks and defensive weakness threads connect to his recurring banks and Fed commentary.

quotes.q: Ignore the headlines, put the newspaper away, and focus on the price action.
Wells has a culture of screwing up the quarter every four to five quarters. Like clockwork.

questions: If leadership is this concentrated in semis, what happens to passive portfolios when the AI story hits its first real speed bump?
Has gold permanently lost its safe haven role, or does it recover once the war premium unwinds?
Does the melt-up scenario require the war to end, or just for headlines to keep being ignored?

title: FICO’s Monopoly is Fading & Consumers Are the Winners w/ Kelsey Zhu | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 59
thesis: Zhu argues FICO has abused a monopoly to the point of breaking it. The company raised the price of a mortgage credit score pull from about 60 cents in 2022 to 10 dollars, roughly a 1,500% increase over 5 years, and because a single mortgage can involve five or six pulls across three bureaus and multiple lenders, the cost compounds through the whole origination chain. That pricing has angered the entire lending ecosystem just as a real alternative arrived: Vantage Score has been validated for mortgage underwriting while FICO's own next-generation 10-T score has not, so lenders finally have somewhere to go. Zhu rates FICO underperform because share loss is coming and consensus estimates do not reflect it. Zooming out to the rest of her coverage, she ranks financial information companies by moat: Verisk, effectively a monopoly in insurance loss cost data, and MSCI, a beneficiary of passive investing, are the best businesses, while FactSet is the most problematic because its end users, active managers, are no longer growing, and she sees AI as a cost tailwind for the group rather than the existential threat the market fears.
pushback: Eisman forces the arithmetic and the how at every step. He makes Zhu walk pull by pull through what FICO actually earns on a single mortgage, from 60 cents times three bureaus times three lenders through the five or six pulls of a full origination, and he pins down that the flat fee model is now 10 dollars against Vantage's roughly one dollar, drawing her dry line that ten dollars is nine dollars more than a dollar. He also presses on the confusion itself, the pricing grid and success fee that lenders and investors cannot model, treating opacity as evidence of a company behaving badly. In his closer he directly challenges management's public claim of zero expected share loss, saying he finds it hard to believe from a company that has infuriated its entire customer base.
evidence: FICO mortgage score pricing went from about $0.60 a pull in 2022 to $10, a roughly 1,500% increase over 5 years
A mortgage applicant shopping three lenders can generate five or six pulls, each pulled from all three bureaus, with FICO paid on every one
Vantage Score has been validated for use in mortgage underwriting; FICO 10-T has not been validated or implemented
Vantage Score pricing sits around a dollar a pull against FICO's $10 flat fee model
Two years ago investors asked Zhu whether score pricing could reach $50; now they ask whether it goes to $1
Verisk's loss cost segment, its largest, is basically a monopoly in P&C insurance data
shift: The two converge rather than clash: Zhu holds her underperform on share loss and too-high estimates, and Eisman ends more negative than he started, committing to watch the next several quarters for evidence of share erosion. The one gap left open is AI, where Zhu thinks the threat to information services is overblown and Eisman counters that no one will have real clarity for at least a year.
context: This is the show's cleanest case study in its recurring rule that monopoly pricing abuse eventually invites its own destruction, and in the May 15 wrap Eisman disclosed he is short FICO, calling the price hikes among the most egregious monopolistic acts he has seen. The episode also extends the show's AI-and-software anxiety thread, since the whole financial information sector trades as software and carries the same negative AI narrative discussed with Rasgon and Marcus.

quotes.q: They have angered the entire lending market and they're going to lose market share.

questions: How fast does Vantage Score actually take mortgage share once lenders can switch, and what does the first quarter of evidence look like?
Can FICO ever get 10-T validated in time to blunt the bureaus' attack, or has the window closed?
If AI turns out to threaten rather than help information services, do even the Verisk and MSCI moats hold?

title: Conspiracy of Credit Part 1
thesis: Eisman argues that the United States has not had a credit cycle induced recession since 2008, and that the credit built in the interval is both concentrated and unobservable. The Fed's post crisis regime forced banks to delever and to stop making risky loans, so lending growth migrated to private credit, where it sits behind a veil of privacy that he treats as a synonym for secrecy. Because markets are clearing mechanisms, hidden risk cannot be priced, and unpriced risk resolves through panic rather than repricing. The specific error is concentration: rates fell in 2018, the SaaS subscription model turned software into a predictable cash cow, and private equity and private credit piled into the same bet through 2022, only for AI to threaten the value of exactly those assets. His conclusion is a real recession risk without 2008 scale systemic risk, because the loans are not resecuritized and the banks are capitalized.
pushback: A solo lecture, and he raises the strongest counter himself: this is not 2008. He sizes 2006 subprime at 600 billion resecuritized into CDOs at perhaps ten times that, giving trillions of exposure, against a roughly 1.8 trillion private credit industry with almost no resecuritization, and he says plainly he expects losses and perhaps a recession rather than a total disaster. He then partly undercuts that comfort by noting the banks are lenders to the funds anyway, and that the equity underneath may itself be borrowed.
evidence: Roughly 300 billion of bank lending extended to private credit funds, the regulated system's workaround
Public BDC leverage capped at two to one, with other private credit vehicles able to lever further
Blue Owl's flagship OCIC fund, about 36 billion in assets, receiving first quarter 2026 redemption requests of 21.9% of assets, with the 3.3 billion OTIC also elevated
Retail facing funds gating redemptions at 5% to 7% per quarter and taking requests above the gate all year
2006 subprime volume of 600 billion, resecuritized into CDOs at roughly ten times that amount
At least 25% of direct lending loans made to software companies bought by private equity between 2018 and 2022
The Wall Street Journal analysis of March 30 showing software loans booked under the end industry, so healthcare software counted as healthcare
shift: Nothing converges because nothing is contested. The lecture moves from a claim about opacity to a claim about concentration, and lands softer than the framing implies: a bad credit cycle with real losses, not a systemic event.
context: The spine of the show's private credit thread, and the piece that connects it to the K shaped economy and to AI capex. AI is cast here not as the capex story but as the thing destroying the collateral behind the last cycle's software LBOs, which is the sharpest version of that argument the show has made.

quotes.q: Labeling the rotten eggs differently doesn't change the number of rotten eggs.
Even expensive, well-paid cows prefer to join the herd.

questions: If the true software exposure is above the disclosed 25%, at what level does his not systemic verdict break?
Do redemption gates buy the funds time to work out the software book, or just concentrate the run into the next quarter?

title: A Conspiracy Of Credit Master Class: Part 2
thesis: Eisman's argument is that the bond market's apparent complexity is mostly a language barrier maintained by the small group of institutions that run it. Every industry has a mafia that sets the rules and the lingo, and the lingo keeps insiders in and outsiders out, but underneath it the fixed income world is common sense plus arithmetic. He then builds the toolkit: bonds priced off the treasury curve, the curve sloping because time is risk, ratings functioning as the sole subjective input in an objective market and therefore setting rather than influencing price, and credit judged on cash flow, collateral, covenants and character. The payoff is deferred to part three, where the same tools explain how subprime securitization nearly ended the system.
pushback: None is aired. The nearest thing to a counterweight is his handling of the repeat question. He asks directly whether today's unregulated private lenders are a historical rhyme with 2008, answers maybe, and then narrows it: exposure today is significant and deep in certain industries rather than unlimited, so there will be pain without a rerun.
evidence: Treasuries treated as the risk free benchmark for all bond pricing even after Moody's and S&P dropped the United States from triple A
The ordering he keeps returning to, treasury yields below high grade corporates, high grade below high yield, with the gap defined as the spread
Rating agencies described as the only subjective element in a totally objective mathematical market, with institutions positioning ahead of downgrades
The four Cs of credit analysis, cash flow, collateral, covenants and character
The amortization worked example, a five year bond at par of 1,000 dollars with a 7% coupon paying 70 dollars a year and returning principal only at maturity
Residential mortgages as the self amortizing exception, where each payment retires interest and principal together
Private loans described as having very little to no liquidity, leaving a lender in a thirty year contract stuck
shift: Nothing moves, by design. This is instruction rather than argument. The one live position carried through is that the current cycle rhymes with 2008 without matching it, held from the opening minute to the close.
context: The bridge episode of the private credit series and the show's clearest statement of its own method, that opacity is usually vocabulary plus incentive rather than genuine difficulty. It also sets up the life insurance thread with Tom Gober, which he names here as an example of what may be coming.

quotes.q: Lingo keeps insiders in and outsiders out.
The ratings of the ratings agencies don't impact the price, they set the price.

questions: If ratings set prices and agencies are structurally late, what marks private credit loans that no agency rates at all?
Which covenants in current direct lending deals would actually bind a sponsor that decides to walk away?

title: Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60
thesis: Brackett explains the puzzle in the episode title: the war has closed the Strait of Hormuz and taken roughly 20% of world oil production off the market, yet energy stocks are down since the invasion. His answer is structural neglect plus hope. Energy is only 4% of the S&P 500, so generalist portfolio managers consumed by AI can buy Exxon and forget the sector, and oil prices themselves are capped by the market's persistent hope that the war ends soon. His framework for owning the group is cash return rather than commodity heroics: Exxon and Chevron each return 30 to 50 billion dollars a year in dividends and buybacks, and those yields should be compared to TIPS, not treasuries, because commodity producers are inflation protected. For risk-averse investors he points to toll-booth midstream models, especially Cheniere, which trades near an 8% free cash flow yield against the roughly 5% where S&P midstream gas peers settle, with no price risk and no geopolitical risk.
pushback: Eisman keeps forcing the disconnect between the physical shock and the share prices, pressing on why oil is not far higher with a fifth of production offline, and on the political wildcard of the UAE dropping out of OPEC this year. He also plays devil's advocate on valuation logic, asking why anyone takes a 3% dividend when treasuries pay five, which draws Brackett's TIPS comparison, and he probes whether the transparently great EOG becomes a takeover target, which Brackett deflects into the premium problem of great companies being expensive stocks. In closing, Eisman reframes the whole sector more harshly than his guest: these are trading vehicles for value investors, bought at commodity-price lows and sold into excitement, not long-term growth holdings.
evidence: The closing of the strait took roughly 20% of world oil production out of the market, yet oil prices are lower than that shock implies
Energy is only about 4% of the S&P 500, so generalists can own Exxon alone and ignore the rest
Exxon pays roughly $20 billion a year in dividends plus 20 to 25 billion in buybacks; Exxon and Chevron each return 30 to 50 billion a year while still growing
Cheniere trades near an 8% free cash flow yield versus about 5% for midstream gas companies inside the S&P 500
The UAE dropped out of OPEC this year, a break in the cartel's structure since the 1970s
Exxon outperformed in January and February and has fallen since the invasion, tracking hope of a quick end to the war
shift: No real disagreement to resolve, but Eisman walks away with a sharper version of the cyclicality rule than Brackett offered: buy these stocks only when the commodity has collapsed and nobody will touch them, and expect strong production for a year or two as countries restock inventories after the war's destruction. Brackett holds his likes, Exxon, select drillers like Diamondback, EOG at a price, and Cheniere as the safest risk-adjusted return in the group.
context: The episode is the war's commodity chapter in a spring dominated by the Iran conflict, and it pairs with the Arment defense episode the following week as the two sectors the war should be repricing. It also feeds Eisman's running argument that the AI trade has starved every other sector of attention and capital, with energy the clearest orphan.

quotes.q: Don't compare the yields you get from a commodity company to government yields. Compare them to TIPS.
EOG is so great and almost so transparently great that it's typically an expensive stock.

questions: If 20% of world production offline cannot lift energy stocks, what shock would?
Does the UAE leaving OPEC mark the beginning of the cartel's unraveling and a structurally lower oil price?
When the war ends and restocking demand fades, does the sector give back everything except the cash-return names?

title: How Silicon Valley Took Over the Defense Industry with Peter Arment | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 61
thesis: Arment's argument is that a single dinner reshaped the defense industry and its consequences are now reversing. At the Last Supper at the Pentagon on July 21, 1993, the government told roughly 60 prime contractors to consolidate for the peace dividend, and the survivors became enormous, profitable and slow. Now, with defense budgets at a trillion dollars and rising and wars in Iran and Ukraine, an unprecedented wave of venture capital and private equity money that entered between 2020 and 2024 is funding nimble startups that build low-cost, purpose-built systems faster and cheaper than the primes can respond. The result is a share shift away from exquisite platforms, exemplified by the F-35 at 80 million dollars or more per aircraft, toward affordable mass like drones, effectively swinging the industry back toward its pre-1993 structure. In aerospace, Boeing's spend-billions-to-lose-billions-to-make-billions model has been diluted by its capital raise, and the quiet winners are nuclear-exposed suppliers Curtiss-Wright and BWX Technologies, riding both defense demand and commercial reactor life extension.
pushback: Eisman pushes on cost and relevance rather than direction. He gets Arment to admit the F-35's real unit cost exceeds Lockheed's quoted 80 million, and the two build the case together that for a customer like Taiwan, with China at most 117 miles away, cheap drones make more sense than a hugely expensive F-35 acquisition. On Boeing, Eisman forces the dilution math into the open: a company once capable of about 40 dollars of free cash flow per share is now headed to about 20 because of the capital raised to repair the balance sheet, which caps the upside even if the story works.
evidence: The industry had about 60 prime contractors in the 1980s; the July 21, 1993 Last Supper dinner at the Pentagon triggered consolidation to a handful
Defense budgets are around a trillion dollars and going higher
The F-35 costs at least 80 million dollars each; at 156 aircraft a year the program approaches 2,000 delivered by the early 2030s, more than a third of the total buy
The longest distance between China and Taiwan is 117 miles, undercutting the case for expensive long-range platforms in that theater
Boeing roughly doubled the cost of what it expected to spend developing the 787
Boeing's free cash flow potential has fallen from about $40 per share to about $20 after dilution
Curtiss-Wright services the installed base of 94 US reactors, an aftermarket business now growing mid teens as plants extend from 40 to 60 to 80 year licenses
shift: Eisman ends where Arment pointed him but with sharper portfolio conclusions: not much to do in the primes, real interest in the nimble drone names like AeroVironment, and a commitment to do his own further work on Curtiss-Wright and BWX Technologies, which he calls the most interesting companies discussed. Arment concedes nothing because Eisman never contested the thesis, only the price tags.
context: The war backdrop that lifted oil in the Brackett episode gets its defense counterpart here, and the episode adds a new instance of a recurring Eisman pattern: government-engineered consolidation creating incumbents too big to pivot, the same overconsolidation critique he applies elsewhere to monopolies like FICO. The nuclear supplier thread also links forward to the AI power constraint discussed with Rasgon, where reactor restarts feed data center demand.

quotes.q: We have to spend billions to lose billions to make billions.
Lockheed Martin will tell you 80 million. I'll say it's more than that.

questions: How much of the trillion-dollar budget actually migrates from the primes to the new defense tech companies, and how fast?
Do the venture-backed entrants survive a peace settlement in Iran or Ukraine, or does the capital wave recede with the headlines?
Can the nuclear aftermarket names stay reasonably valued once the market notices the defense plus data center double tailwind?

title: Inside the Hidden Consumer Crisis with Lakshmi Ganapathi
thesis: Ganapathi's argument is that the clean consumer credit data is evidence of suppression rather than health. Since 2020 lenders have run extend and pretend, holding borrowers current as long as a minimum payment arrives, which spares the lender from recognizing a default, marking to market or raising provisions, any of which would read as a panic signal. So the gap between reported credit quality and actual household condition keeps widening, and it shows up instead in usage data: buy now pay later funding groceries and rent. Her historical claim is that this is the normal sequence, from Japan in 1987 and 1988 through 2007 and 2008, where a lender breaks first and the consumer appears only as the second order effect. Eisman accepts the mechanism and applies the same denial logic to private credit's software loans.
pushback: Eisman opens by pressing her hard with the data. He says he went through nonaccruals with a fine tooth comb for the first time in years, found them flat on both the consumer and commercial books, notes every management flagged it and even Jamie Dimon conceded no issues so far, and insists the numbers are the numbers. He does not abandon that. He forces her to argue outside the bank data rather than dispute it, and she concedes the surface is clean before arguing the surface is the problem.
evidence: Flat nonaccruals across consumer and commercial books at every reporting bank
Roughly 45 million buy now pay later users, with 30% to 50% having used it at some point
29% of buy now pay later users buying groceries with it, up from 14% two years earlier, and 13% using it for rent
MUFG seeking to move 2 billion off its book via synthetic risk transfer to insurance companies
Roughly 11% of private credit loans refinancing next year, rising to 20% after, into software marks down more than half
Banks funding private credit through warehouse and direct lending, which reaches buy now pay later books through forward flow agreements
Her short list, FICO, AutoZone and Dorman on invoice factoring and receivables, GPI in used cars, Wingstop and DoorDash
shift: Both sides give ground and meet. Eisman keeps the bank data intact and stops treating it as a verdict on the consumer, and Ganapathi concedes the stress has not surfaced in credit yet. They converge fully on private credit: the software refinancing wall arrives next year, sponsors will either add equity or walk, and until then it is noise.
context: This is the K shaped economy and the private credit thread arriving at the same door. The show has argued for months that headline credit metrics describe the top half of the distribution, and here that argument gets a mechanism, extend and pretend, and a tell, installment plans for groceries. It also links the bank, private credit and insurance chains into one exposure.

quotes.q: The data is clean on the surface. And that's exactly what we consider as a problem.
The numbers are the numbers are the numbers.

questions: What breaks extend and pretend, a regulator, a funding cost, or a lender that decides to reserve first?
If sponsors walk from the software loans rather than adding equity, who ends up holding the companies?

title: Is AI a Bubble? Gary Marcus on What Could Break the Story | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 62
thesis: Marcus's argument runs from cognitive science to unit economics. LLMs are sophisticated next-word predictors that memorize and pattern match but fail under distribution shift, and the hallucination problem he flagged in 2001 remains unsolved despite a quarter century of promises that more data would fix it. Around December 2024 the labs discovered, privately and partly publicly, that scaling was no longer delivering the expected returns, yet capex keeps climbing on FOMO, with single companies spending on the order of 180 billion dollars. The deeper crack is economic: because inference runs on massive GPU fleets in the cloud rather than on hardware users already own, every token has a real cost, and the companies have been serving an all-you-can-eat buffet at slim or negative margins that agents make dramatically worse just as they need clean numbers to IPO. If medium-sized models plus tools and symbolic AI turn out to be the right architecture, the giant data centers may never earn their keep, and the industry collectively cannot generate the revenue its spending requires.
pushback: Eisman mounts the strongest bull rebuttal he can, explicitly through his subprime lens. He points out that Nvidia just reported 85% revenue growth, accelerating from 65% two quarters ago, and says that if he wanted to short this story like he shorted subprime, he could not make the argument right now, because the biggest company on earth is accelerating and its customers, Google, Meta and Amazon, are not stupid people. He then forces the mechanism question: subprime broke when the end investor stopped buying the paper, so what is the analogous switch here? His own candidate is the move to real token pricing, where customers simply refuse to pay; Marcus accepts that as plausible and starts to offer his own scenario just as the free feed cuts to premium.
evidence: Nvidia revenue grew 85% in the latest quarter versus 65% two quarters ago, so the buildout is accelerating, not slowing
Marcus identified the hallucination problem in 2001 and published on distribution shift in 1998; both remain unsolved
Scaling returns visibly flattened around December 2024, when labs stopped getting the expected gains from bigger models
One company is spending about 180 billion dollars on AI infrastructure, which Marcus calls lunacy
Token-serving margins are slim or negative, and agents multiply usage, so growth deepens the losses
Agents also consume heavy CPU time alongside GPUs, which is helping Intel and hints that the data center mix bet may be wrong
shift: A genuine partial convergence: Marcus concedes the bull case is a bet with a nonzero chance of paying off, and Eisman concedes he cannot short the story today despite finding the spending incomprehensible. Both agree the resolution test is about a year away, when it becomes clear whether tokens can be priced profitably. Neither yields on the core: Marcus still calls it a low-probability bet, Eisman still refuses to fight 85% revenue growth.
context: This is the show's clearest statement of the AI capex and returns dilemma, sitting directly between the bullish Rasgon semiconductor episode a week later and Eisman's wrap-level warnings that hyperscalers now need public equity markets to fund a trillion dollars of annual capex. It also launches the token pricing and addiction-business-model thread that dominates the June wraps, where Eisman likens subsidized AI usage to Uber-style dependency building.

quotes.q: What I've heard for a quarter century is, oh, Gary, give us a little more data and we'll solve all these problems.
I want to short this story like I shorted subprime. I couldn't make that argument right now.

questions: When token subsidies end and real pricing arrives, do enterprise customers pay up or walk away?
If medium-sized models plus tools win, who is left holding the depreciation on the giant data centers?
What is the AI equivalent of the subprime end investor whose exit stops the whole machine?

title: The AI Semiconductor Boom and What Could End It with Stacy Rasgon | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 63
thesis: Rasgon argues the AI trade has gone into overdrive since his last appearance seven months ago and is now dragging everything along with it, inside semis and out. Demand for compute is accelerating faster than the exponentially growing supply, which is why rental prices on even old GPUs are rising rather than falling and why he dismisses the depreciation worry: if demand ever falls enough to strand old compute, everything is broken anyway. The bottlenecks have migrated to memory and CPUs, the latter because agentic AI needs heavy CPU time alongside GPUs, and Nvidia has recut its disclosure into hyperscale versus non-hyperscale to reflect where demand lives. The only real long-term risk he sees is that returns on AI disappoint, in which case the whole thing is a shell game with nowhere to hide, but he judges it far too early for that question to bite, so he stays bullish while flagging power, not chips, as the binding constraint, with China able to throw up coal plants while the US resorts to on-site generation and restarting Three Mile Island.
pushback: Eisman keeps steering the conversation to the systemic downside, getting Rasgon to spell out that if there is no return on AI, everything comes crumbling down in semis and out of semis, with AI capex cited as roughly 75% of last year's GDP growth and the railroad buildout the only historical comparison by share of the economy. He also drills into the how of the CPU story, making Rasgon explain the GB300 NVL72 rack, 72 GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs, and why agents change the compute mix, and he presses on Intel, where Rasgon stays unimpressed, noting 18A yields near zero at the comparable point and calling the company still not great despite packaging demand and foundry rumors.
evidence: Nvidia reported 85% revenue growth versus 65% two quarters ago, so the buildout is accelerating
Nvidia's flagship GB300 NVL72 rack carries 72 GPUs and 36 Arm-based Grace CPUs, and agentic AI is raising CPU content per rack
AI capex was roughly 75% of US GDP growth last year, a share comparable only to the railroad buildout
Rental prices for older-generation GPUs are rising, not falling, because demand outruns even exponentially growing compute supply
Nvidia recut its data center disclosure into hyperscale versus non-hyperscale customers
Intel's 18A yields were close to zero at this point in its life, and hoped-for foundry wins like Apple would start small
Nvidia the stock is up only 14% this year while memory and CPU bottleneck plays have led the group
shift: Nothing converges because there is little disagreement to start: Eisman ends still bullish alongside Rasgon, noting that the bottleneck stocks have run enormously yet earnings rose faster, so multiples actually contracted. Both hold that disappointing AI returns are the eventual kill switch, and both judge it too early in the story for that to matter now.
context: The bull counterweight to the Gary Marcus episode a week earlier, framed by Eisman's opening line that semis are now the center of the universe the way financials were before 2008. The power constraint and nuclear restart discussion ties back to the Arment episode's reactor suppliers, and the shell game exchange feeds Eisman's June wrap thesis that hyperscalers have become capital-intensive hardware companies asking shareholders to fund the buildout.

quotes.q: If it turns out there's no return on AI, it's all a shell game. Everything's coming crumbling down, in semis and out of semis.
The center of the universe right now is semiconductors, because that is where the entire AI infrastructure is being built out.

questions: How would investors actually detect disappointing AI returns before the capex stops, given every current signal is accelerating demand?
Does the CPU and memory bottleneck trade keep outrunning Nvidia itself, or does leadership rotate back?
Can the US grid and on-site generation scale fast enough, or does power cap the buildout regardless of chip supply?

title: Is Private Equity Destroying the Life Insurance Industry? | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 64
thesis: Booked explicitly as a second opinion after former insurance examiner Tom Gober's alarming earlier interview, Gallagher argues that private equity's takeover of life insurance is riskier than the old model but not recklessly so. Since Apollo bought the platform that became Athene in 2012, followed by KKR's Global Atlantic, Carlyle's Corebridge stake and Blackstone's minority-stake model, the alternative managers have earned roughly 100 basis points more than traditional insurers, whose zero-loss-cost investing he considers overly conservative rather than prudent. He went bond by bond through the top 30 to 40 private credit positions as a gut check and did not find risk that scares him at the big platforms, though he does worry about smaller aggressive sponsors. The industry's real historical wounds came from long-tail products, variable annuities hedging 20 year liabilities with 3 month options and secondary guarantee universal life priced for mid-to-high single digit lapses that ran at 1%, and that distrust is why the sector trades at 3 to 5 times earnings. Offshore reinsurance persists because regulators accommodate it rather than lose jurisdiction entirely.
pushback: Eisman pushes twice. First on the regulatory arbitrage: he asks flatly how offshore reinsurance is even allowed, and Gallagher's answer, that punitive regimes accommodate rather than watch companies exit their jurisdiction, leaves the accommodation looking uncomfortably circular. Second and harder on capital return: if these stocks trade at 3 to 5 times earnings, the companies should be buying back stock like crazy, and Gallagher agrees they should but notes even the disciplined ones like Corebridge and Equitable only run buybacks around 8% of market cap a year, while Lincoln must first refinance a preferred costing around 9 to 12% before it can get aggressive in 2027. Eisman openly says he was surprised by Gallagher's comfort with the private equity insurers.
evidence: Private equity's entry began with Apollo's 2012 purchase of a fixed index annuity writer from Aviva that became Athene; Apollo is the biggest player, KKR second via Global Atlantic, bought from Goldman Sachs
Alternative managers earn about 100 basis points more on portfolios than traditional insurers running zero-loss-cost models
Gallagher reviewed the top 30 to 40 private credit positions bond by bond as an eye test on the big platforms
Secondary guarantee universal life assumed mid-to-high single digit lapse rates; actual lapses ran about 1% once rates collapsed
Parts of the sector trade at 3 to 5 times earnings on decades of distrust from long-tail blowups
Corebridge and Equitable repurchase roughly 8% of market cap a year; Lincoln is about a year from aggressive buybacks and must deal with a preferred costing around 9 to 12% by 2027
Apollo and Athene's net interest margins have been squeezed for a couple of years as low-cost liabilities rolled off while retail private credit flows turned negative
shift: Eisman moves, at least partially: he came in primed by Gober's warnings and admits surprise that Gallagher, whom he has known and trusted for decades, is comfortable with the large alternative insurers, reserving his worry for smaller aggressive players. He still concludes there is not much to buy in the public names, but reclassifies the sector from danger zone to essential monitoring post for the broader alternatives complex. Gallagher holds his ground throughout.
context: The deliberate counterweight in the show's private credit arc: Gober prosecuted, Gallagher defends, and Eisman triangulates, consistent with his masterclass thesis that private credit will produce losses but not a 2008 rerun because banks are well capitalized. The retail private credit outflows and spread squeeze Gallagher describes echo the redemption-gate stories Eisman tracks weekly at FSK and Partners Group.

quotes.q: How do you win in a commodity market? You get bigger. You have scale, you have distribution advantages.
People basically just don't trust these companies. And that's why some of these stocks sell at three to five times earnings.

questions: If regulators tolerate offshore reinsurance only to avoid losing jurisdiction, what happens when a Bermuda-sided balance sheet actually breaks?
Are the smaller alternative-sponsored insurers Gallagher worries about big enough collectively to infect the large platforms?
Why will managements start buying back stock aggressively at 3 to 5 times earnings when they have declined to for years?

title: The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky
thesis: Zipursky's argument is that the addiction suits against Meta and Google turn entirely on framing. Section 230C has been read extremely broadly for twenty years, protecting platforms even where the content is plainly harmful, so any claim built on what users posted loses. The plaintiffs therefore recast the platform as a defective product whose design knowingly addicts adolescents, which routes around 230 and lands in a body of product liability law that has been expanding since the privity rule collapsed. He separates the theories by strength: negligence and design defect are legally serious, and public nuisance, the theory plaintiffs' lawyers will push hardest, he considers made up but frightening enough to force settlements. His final point is that nothing is settled, because only two cases have been tried and no appellate court has ruled.
pushback: Eisman keeps testing whether this is genuinely new, and gets a careful no. Zipursky says it is not unique, there is a sprinkling of cases where 230C fails, but it is huge because it is a mass tort with one plaintiff among 1,800 in a single filing. Eisman also challenges the made up charge directly, asking what he actually means by it, and later pushes on jurisdiction, asking how a global company complies with an American injunction, where Zipursky concedes he does not know. Eisman's final push is the bleakest: is litigation the only route left given frozen legislatures, and Zipursky rejects the premise.
evidence: The Los Angeles verdict against Meta of roughly 6 million dollars, argued as negligence and supported by Zuckerberg testimony about a knowingly addictive model
That plaintiff being one of 1,800 in her filing, itself one of scores of similar actions nationally
The Sixth Circuit extending Section 230C to the operator of thedirty.com over user submitted allegations about a Cincinnati woman
The New Mexico case split in two, a consumer fraud phase tried to a jury and an injunctive phase heard by a judge, with the public nuisance phase beginning in May
The injunction seeking an actual algorithm redesign to reduce addictiveness, alongside relief Zipursky calls a fake injunction
