The exploding Coke bottle line, where proving the bottle defective suffices without proving negligence in the inspection process
Zero appellate decisions to date on any of these issues, with every tried case heading up on appeal
shift: Eisman moves and Zipursky holds. Eisman arrives treating the California verdict as a possible inflection and leaves with a much longer time horizon, describing the story as early, multi chapter and unresolved until appeals run. Zipursky holds his split verdict throughout: design defect serious, public nuisance made up, legislation the better road.
context: A rare non financial episode that is still a valuation episode, since an unquantifiable mass tort against the largest platforms is exactly the kind of hidden liability the show hunts for elsewhere in private credit and insurance. It also matches his standing preference for disclosure and rules over litigation as the mechanism that actually changes corporate behaviour.

quotes.q: I think the nuisance theories are kind of made up, but they're so scary that people settle.
There hasn't been one appellate decision yet in this country on any of these issues.

questions: Does the design defect framing survive the first appellate test, or does Section 230 swallow it back up?
If New York's unenforced statute gets its regulations written, does legislation overtake the litigation entirely?

title: The Real State of the American Consumer w/ Three Evercore Analysts | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 65
thesis: Three Evercore analysts give the K-shaped economy its bottom-up confirmation. Palmer's framing device: restaurant spending divides into equal thirds across households under 50,000, 50,000 to 100,000 and over 100,000, so when the low end retrenches and the middle weakens, the damage is visible immediately, and it is: low-end chains like Wendy's and McDonald's struggle while protein-led high-end concepts like Texas Roadhouse and LongHorn comp around 10 to 11%. Binetti's version in retail is barbell survival, Ralph Lauren and Coach at the top and off-price value at the bottom, with an ocean in the middle that is failing even after the best tax refund season since COVID, while Nike's rushed direct-to-consumer pivot destroyed its competitive intelligence and let rivals in. Melich closes the loop: the housing market is locked by 3 to 4% COVID mortgages, killing Home Depot and Lowe's, while the squeezed middle trades down into Walmart, which has also built same-day delivery of anything to anyone that no one else can match. Legacy packaged food, skewed against protein in a GLP-1 world, has no end in sight to its decline.
pushback: With three guests, Eisman plays prosecutor for specificity rather than opposition. He runs Binetti through the murderer's row of broken stocks one at a time, Lululemon, Ulta, Gap, Kohl's, Canada Goose, demanding what is actually wrong with each, and he extracts the admission that Nike's problem became the product itself once competitors seized the moment. He forces Palmer to name one or two names he really likes and really dislikes rather than talk categories, and he challenges the housing paradox with Melich, that unlocking the market should mean lower prices yet prices keep rising, which Melich resolves as pure supply shortage against plentiful demand from household formation.
evidence: Restaurant spending splits into roughly equal thirds across income cohorts under $50,000, $50,000 to $100,000, and over $100,000
This year saw the best tax refund season since COVID, and the middle-income retail cohort still failed to deliver
LongHorn is comping around 10 to 11% same-store sales growth while Olive Garden struggles, the protein versus non-protein divide in one company
Nike's direct-to-consumer shift cost it visibility into head-to-head brand choices in multi-brand retail, and a returning veteran is finding the turnaround slow
Homeowners locked into 3 to 4% COVID mortgages cannot sell against 7% rates, freezing housing turnover and inventory
Home Depot's growth hope rests on the pro segment and an aging housing stock, not on a housing recovery
Walmart can now deliver essentially anything to anyone the same day, a capability no competitor matches
shift: Eisman ends by synthesizing rather than conceding: the middle is cracking, which is bad news for the consumer overall but great news for Walmart, and he leaves calling Walmart the big positive story of the episode while writing off packaged food and housing-linked retail entirely. None of the three analysts moves; each holds his subsector read and Eisman adopts all three into his K-shaped framework.
context: The capstone of the show's K-shaped economy thread, giving company-level texture to what Lakshmi Ganapathi's buy now, pay later work and the Walmart and Target wrap commentary had sketched from the top down. The locked housing market analysis extends Eisman's standing housing affordability theme, including his own advice that a home is shelter, not an investment, and the Walmart trade-down story becomes a fixture of his subsequent market commentary.

quotes.q: There's an ocean in the middle that's not doing so well.
Everything's a protein world. If you're not on team protein, it's harder for you.

questions: How long can Walmart's gains from middle-class trade-down outrun the overall weakening of the consumer that produces them?
Is Nike's problem fixable brand execution or a permanent loss of share to structurally stronger competitors?
What finally unlocks the housing market if neither falling prices nor rising supply is anywhere in sight?

title: Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands
thesis: Glass House has spent its life as the lowest cost cannabis grower in the world while being legally confined to one state. Schedule I status barred interstate commerce, so the company's cost advantage collided with California's saturated wholesale market and capped realized prices near 200 dollars per pound. Reclassifying medical cannabis to Schedule III opens interstate sales between DEA compliant operators where states agree, and opens export to a European medical market with almost no domestic cultivation. Because the incremental cost of serving those markets is essentially shipping, the price gap between 200 in California and 800 to 1,000 elsewhere converts almost entirely into margin. Eisman's own arithmetic on the follow up episode turns that into a stock worth several times its price.
pushback: Eisman does not challenge the growth story so much as force it into numbers. He repeatedly interrupts to pin down concrete figures, making DeCourcy restate that Glass House is the largest cannabis grower in the world, extracting the 80% wholesale split, and pressing on why New York fetches 800 when California fetches 200 until he gets the supply and demand answer. He also presses on the exchange listing question and gets only that discussions are ongoing. His own disclosure runs as a constant hedge: he owns it, he is happy, and he says three times he is not trying to sell it to anyone.
evidence: Medical cannabis reclassified from Schedule I to Schedule III on April 23
Expedited DEA hearing on recreational cannabis set for June 29, required by law to conclude by mid July
First quarter revenue of 40.5 million dollars, roughly 80% wholesale
Production cost near 100 dollars per pound against a California wholesale price around 200
Average selling price of 800 to 1,000 dollars per pound in other US medical markets
Capacity of about 1.4 million pounds of biomass with one greenhouse still vacant, versus roughly 700,000 pounds in a normal year
Curaleaf and TerrAscend uplisted to the TSX on non Schedule I revenue as small as 200,000 dollars per year
shift: Nothing converges because nothing diverged. Eisman came in a shareholder and left more convinced, ending on the claim that operating margins could travel from about 50% toward 80% to 90%. The only ground he concedes is the one he keeps naming himself, that this is speculative, that regulatory hurdles remain, and that anything can happen in cannabis.
context: This is the show's clearest non AI idea, a pure regulatory arbitrage sitting outside the K shaped consumer debate and the capex cycle. It also picks up the exchange access thread, since the same institutional plumbing that shapes who can own a stock shows up wherever Eisman discusses market structure. He returns to it a week later inside his portfolio episode, where the qualitative case becomes a valuation table.

quotes.q: We are the largest cannabis grower in the world.
There are no extra costs here other than shipping. It's just all margin.

questions: Does recreational cannabis actually reach Schedule III after the June hearing, and how many states then permit inbound supply?
Can Glass House fund its expansion without an equity raise that dilutes the margin story?
Once institutions can buy the stock, does European medical demand absorb California volume at anything close to 1,000 dollars a pound?

title: The Market's Biggest Warning Signs Right Now with Todd Sohn | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 66
thesis: Sohn argues that charts are the most efficient summary of what money is actually doing, and right now every chart tells the same story: the market has collapsed into a single tech trade. Information technology alone is about 38% of the S&P 500, and once you add Google and Amazon, which sit outside the official tech sector, the AI complex is well over half the index. Because most funds are market cap weighted, anyone who owns the S&P, Russell 1000 Growth or a thematic fund is stacked with the same handful of names, so index ownership no longer equals diversification. Flows confirm it: money pours into tech ETFs and into the booming leveraged ETF space, industrials only attract money because of the power story, which is tech in another costume, while financials, cyclicals, defensives, gold and Bitcoin see indifference or outflows. His prescription is not to sell but to look under the hood and know how much of one theme you actually own.
pushback: Eisman plays translator and stress-tester rather than opponent. He forces Sohn to define RSI and overbought in plain English, makes him defend the claim that a consolidating semiconductor chart is buyable rather than broken, and deliberately tries to construct a bull case for REITs, to which Sohn answers, good luck, before both concede that at under 2% of the S&P the sector is too small for a portfolio manager to care about. On Bitcoin, Eisman offers his own thesis, that the young traders who made it cool have decamped to prediction markets like Kalshi, and Sohn accepts it as a good point.
evidence: Information technology is about 38% of the S&P 500, and with Google and Amazon added the tech complex is well over 50%
There are roughly 5,000 ETFs, more ETFs than there are listed stocks, though mutual funds still outnumber both
Leveraged ETFs give two to three times exposure, and leveraged single-stock ETFs did not exist until 2022
REITs are about 2% or less of the S&P, and the REIT index holds only about 30 stocks
Flows show money going into industrials on the power story but essentially none into financials
Money is coming out of both gold and Bitcoin ETFs, leaving a low bar for both assets
Google's chart still looks good while Meta, Oracle, Microsoft and Amazon charts range from mediocre to bad
shift: No disagreement to resolve; the episode ends with Eisman radicalizing Sohn's flow data into his own darker conclusion. Sohn's parting advice is to know what you own; Eisman closes that if the tech trade ever reverses there will be no place to hide, since even the diversifiers have become the same bet.
context: This is the chart-based version of the argument Torsten Slok makes economically two weeks later in Ep 68: everyone is overindexed to AI whether they know it or not. It also extends the show's running crypto scepticism, with the Kalshi-killed-Bitcoin thesis that resurfaces in the August 14 wrap, and the power-is-just-tech observation that frames the Ben Kallo episode.

quotes.q: Pay attention to what you own. It's a bull market, but you might be loaded up on more exposure than you think.
If the stuff ever reverses, there'll be no place to hide.

questions: What level of interest rates or AI disappointment actually triggers the rotation the flow data says nobody is positioned for?
Is the boom in leveraged and single-stock ETFs a sign of healthy retail participation or late-cycle speculation?
If financials see no flows despite strong earnings, is that the contrarian bullish setup Sohn hints at?

title: Steve Eisman Reveals His Personal Portfolio: Every Position Explained
thesis: Eisman's method is to buy a story rather than a chart, size it fully at once, and hold until the thesis breaks rather than trade around it. He argues that the AI weighting in his book, seven of 16 names, only looks aggressive until measured against an index that is 37% infotech and closer to 50% counting Google and Amazon. Within AI he is suspicious of the software layer, because price cutting this early implies no moat and the industry already undercharges for tokens, so he prefers the physical bottleneck: power, grid buildout and equipment with multi year backlogs. Around that he holds value names, monopolies and duopolies he calls great franchises, and a small speculative tail. He then makes the whole structure falsifiable by naming four conditions that would force him to rebuild it.
pushback: This is a solo lecture, and the strongest objection is the one he raises against himself. He states that at least 50% of AI spending traces back to Anthropic and OpenAI, that both burn billions and depend on venture funding, that OpenAI is the weaker of the two, and that over 50% of Oracle's data center backlog is tied to OpenAI. He follows it with the admission that this is a guess. He also volunteers mistakes: not buying Cisco alongside Arista, bad timing on Charter and Meritage, and notes that Chris Hohn exited Microsoft entirely while he only trimmed.
evidence: Sixteen long positions across five themes, at the low end of his usual 15 to 30 range after pruning
Infotech at 37% of the S&P 500, rising toward 50% once Google and Amazon are included
Over 50% of Oracle's data center backlog tied to OpenAI, per his estimate
Arista down 14% for insufficiently raising guidance
GE Vernova at 45 times 2026 EPS estimates, Quanta at 50 times 2026 earnings
Charter bundling cable and mobile at 100 dollars a month versus 180 to 200 for competitors
Glass House scenarios at 45%, 55% and 65% EBITDA margins on 500 dollars per pound, yielding 40, 49 and 58 dollars a share against a 13 dollar stock
shift: He does not change position during the episode, but he narrows it. He holds the AI infrastructure names on backlog visibility while explicitly downgrading his confidence in AI software economics, and he keeps Microsoft only in reduced size. The closing conditions are the real movement: data center buildout proving harder than expected, corporates retreating on usage cost, the 10 year holding above 4.5% for more than a few weeks, or a weakening economy opening short opportunities.
context: This is the show's inventory episode, where the running themes become positions. AI capex and returns splits into a bullish hardware and power book and a sceptical software book. Rates enter through his 4.5% trigger and through Meritage, bought near tangible book as housing affordability stays strained. The Glass House valuation table brings the previous week's regulatory idea into the same portfolio.

quotes.q: If I think I'm right, I take a full position without leveraging up slowly. If I'm wrong, I sell.
AI might be great for mankind, but it has no or little moats to protect the long-term viability of these franchises.

questions: If OpenAI does hit post IPO trouble, how much of his power and infrastructure book survives the ripple through the backlogs?
How does he distinguish a broken thesis from bad timing in Charter and Meritage, both of which he says he bought too early?
Does Microsoft's June 1 move to charge for token use become the industry norm, or does OpenAI price cutting kill it?

title: Who Wins the Midterms & What It Means for Markets with Dan Clifton | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 67
thesis: Clifton traces everything about the midterms back to April 2, 2025: the tariff announcement was the first moment voters ever turned negative on Trump's handling of the economy, an approval asset that had survived even COVID's 30% GDP contraction. From that break he gets to a likely Democratic House, a genuinely 50/50 Senate, and a Democratic party that, if it wins both chambers, will choose accomplishment over ambition, banking modest healthcare and renewable energy wins to argue for full control in 2028. The same electoral math explains the Fed: Powell is holding his seat through the midterms because if Democrats take the Senate, any successor needs confirmation, which forces Trump toward a mainstream economist and protects the New York Fed, where the balance sheet is run. Finally, he argues data centers are the new fracking, a local-politics fight the industry can win because the tax math overwhelmingly favors host counties.
pushback: The sharpest exchange comes when Clifton predicts a moderate Democratic agenda and Eisman stops him cold, arguing the party has moved much further left than people think and directly challenging the premise; Clifton answers with his four-parties framework, two factions inside each party, to explain why the governing wing would still steer outcomes. At the close Eisman also rejects Clifton's read that Trump can end the Iran war soon, countering that Iran does not really want to negotiate, so the war grinds on.
evidence: Trump's approval rating on the economy went negative for the first time after the April 2, 2025 tariff announcement
The market currently prices about a 50% chance that Democrats win the Senate
The Fed balance sheet has ballooned to about 6 trillion dollars since the GFC, and Clifton expects Kevin Warsh to shrink it by about 1 trillion over time
Data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia pay 40% of the county's education bill, and counties with data centers show falling property tax rates and rising home prices
Clifton's Virginia math: roughly 2,500 dollars a year in property tax savings against perhaps 20 dollars more in electricity costs
The first Clifton episode aired April 4, 2025, the morning after the tariffs, and the market bottomed about three days later
shift: Eisman accepts the electoral map, split government with a Democratic House, but neither side gives ground on the two live disputes: Clifton holds that a winning Democratic party governs from its moderate wing, Eisman holds his doubt, and on Iran Eisman explicitly says he hopes he is wrong but expects the war to last.
context: This continues the show's banks-and-Fed thread by reframing Fed policy as personnel politics, with Warsh's balance sheet ambitions reappearing in the Slok and Trennert episodes. The data-centers-as-new-fracking thesis gives the political leg of the AI capex story that Kallo covers industrially in Ep 69 and Ives and Luria cover as a PR problem in Ep 70.

quotes.q: Our big thesis is data centers are the new fracking.
If you're saying that if the Democrats get both houses they're going to have a moderate agenda, I challenge you on that.

questions: If Democrats do win the Senate, does a confirmation-constrained Fed pick actually change the path of the balance sheet rundown?
Can the tech industry win the local data center fights before moratoriums spread beyond Virginia?
Does an unrestrained J.D. Vance campaign help or fracture the Republican field against Newsom's messy Democratic one?

title: The Bearish Case for Oil and Gold with Queen Anne's Gate Capital
thesis: Kelly argues the market has mistaken wartime distortion for tightness. Before the shooting started oil was at 50 and heading to 40, and the surplus that was forecast for this year did not vanish, it was pushed into late this year and next. Meanwhile roughly 5 million barrels per day of new supply arrives next year against demand growth of perhaps 2.5 million even on generous assumptions, the UAE is adding about 1.5 million now that it sits outside OPEC, and China keeps cutting its own demand. US demand looks healthy only because record distillate and jet fuel exports are filling gaps left by China, the Middle East and Russia, and that flow reverses when the war ends. On gold, O'Flynn's point is that the metal already priced the catastrophe in advance, so the catastrophe itself became a selling event.
pushback: Eisman tests the downside repeatedly rather than accepting it. He asks how low prices can go, reacts to the answer with visible disbelief, and pushes back on the deflation conclusion by asking whether consumers would actually feel it, drawing the concession that gasoline prices fall but the effect probably arrives after year end. He also questions why cheaper oil would show up in inflation at all when electricity, not oil, now drives the US energy bill, and the guests agree the offset is real. On gold he presses the simplest version: why did it not act the way it is supposed to act.
evidence: Oil in the 70s at recording, with Kelly saying the 20s are easily reachable and Eisman summarizing 40 to 50 as her likelier case
Roughly 5 million barrels per day of new supply next year against demand growth of about 2.5 million
The UAE adding around 1.5 million barrels outside OPEC
Iraq, the producer judged most exposed, saying it can restart within two weeks
Gold running from about 2,500 to 5,200 over the prior year, then selling off when the feared event occurred
Crypto's correlation to the Nasdaq at roughly 75%, so it falls on the days it is supposed to hedge
Kelly's background as a Fed economist, 12 years at Tudor, then Kingdon, plus four years advising the Saudi energy minister
shift: Eisman moves toward the bearish oil case and says so in the afterword, noting explicitly that this is a minority position most people reject and that a resolution should arrive within six to nine months. He does not move on gold because he was never on it, having never owned any in his life, and the guests point him toward silver instead. No one defends crypto, so nothing there is contested.
context: A rare episode where the macro call is deflationary rather than inflationary, which cuts against the Fed and rates thread running through the show. It also lands one more blow on the crypto scepticism theme, this time from commodity specialists rather than from Eisman. And the AI capex story intrudes from the side, since data center electricity demand keeps power prices high even if oil collapses.

quotes.q: There's really not anything that you can come up with that makes this a better situation for oil markets right now.
You couldn't find a gold bear anywhere.

questions: If the surplus is this visible to specialists, why is positioning still long, and what unwinds it first?
Does 40 dollar oil actually reach US consumers as disinflation, or do data center driven electricity prices cancel it?
Does silver hold up if gold keeps unwinding, or does the industrial bid go with it?

title: AI Dominates Economy and Markets with Torsten Slok | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 68
thesis: Slok decomposes roughly 2% US GDP growth into three unusual engines: a full percentage point from the AI spending boom, including data centers, energy and the wealth effect on high-end consumption, about 0.3 points from the industrial renaissance of reshored chips, pharma and defense, and roughly 0.9 points from one-off big beautiful bill tax refunds. Because growth comes from these sources rather than traditional rate-sensitive sectors, housing and autos can stay weak while the economy stays strong, and the Fed has little reason to cut. That mix produces a K-shaped economy along three separate axes, wealth, wage growth and inflation exposure, with the bottom of the distribution losing on all three. The kicker is a diversification illusion: with AI dominating the equity indexes and AI data center debt flooding fixed income, a 60/40 portfolio is overindexed to AI on both sides, and software companies with 2021 to 22 vintage debt face a maturity wall in 2028 and 29 if rates stay high.
pushback: Eisman probes rather than disputes, and mostly sharpens the numbers: he forces the arithmetic that half of this year's growth is pure AI spending, presses Slok on whether the industrial renaissance is real given prior guests shrugged at it, and Slok concedes it adds only 0.3 points against AI's full point. Eisman also pushes the tangent that the tax refund leg disappears next year, implying sub 2% baseline growth in 2027, and tests Slok on why China would not weaponize its Treasury holdings, drawing the answer that crashing US demand would crash Chinese exports.
evidence: AI spending contributes about 1 percentage point of roughly 2% GDP growth, a single-sector contribution bigger than housing ever managed
The industrial renaissance adds about 0.3 points to GDP, with the ISM improving over the last five to six months
About 90 basis points of growth comes from big beautiful bill tax refunds that will not repeat next year
Atlanta Fed data shows lower wage growth at the bottom of the income distribution, and New York Fed data shows higher effective inflation there
Software debt vintages originated in 2021 and 22 carry seven-year maturities, creating a refinancing wall in 2028 and 29
Federal debt to GDP is around 100% and on a path toward 175%
shift: Broad agreement deepens into a shared warning. Slok holds his structurally strong but AI-dependent read of the economy, Eisman adopts the overindexation point as the episode's takeaway and pushes it further: the AI story better work, because if it does not, the losses across both stocks and bonds will be mammoth.
context: This is the macro anchor of the show's summer 2026 AI arc, quantifying the K-shaped economy theme Eisman has run since the healthcare series and giving the economic scaffolding for the July 10 wrap's claim that diversification no longer exists. The software maturity wall lands exactly where the private credit worries of Ep 72 and the SaaSpocalypse debate of Ep 70 converge.

quotes.q: Normally GDP growth is at two, and now 1% is coming from the AI spending boom alone.
This AI story better work, because if it doesn't, the losses people are going to experience are going to be mammoth.

questions: What replaces the 90 basis points of tax refund growth when it lapses in 2027?
Can heavily indebted software companies survive the 2028 to 29 maturity wall if Warsh keeps rates high?
Is there any practical way for an ordinary investor to be diversified when both equities and credit are indexed to AI?

title: Beyond Ozempic: The Next Wave of Biotech Winners with Boris Peaker
thesis: Peaker's argument is that biotech's investment map is drawn by economics, not by science. The old technical divide between pharma small molecules and biotech biologics has dissolved, since Pfizer, Merck, Roche and Lilly can now build anything a small company can, leaving size as the only real distinction. What remains is a division of labor: small firms carry drugs toward the finish line and large firms buy them and commercialize, so the recycling of capital through acquisitions is what funds the sector. Within that structure, capital flows to oncology because efficacy reads out fast, prescribers adopt anything marginally better for dying patients, and safety tolerance is high. Fields that lack that economics, notably antibiotics and aging, stay underfunded no matter how badly the drugs are needed.
pushback: Eisman pushes on whether the celebrated wins are actually wins. Told that Revolution's pancreatic drug takes median survival from about 6 months to about 13, and that this is scientifically impressive, he answers that you are still only living for 13 months. He also presses the aging question hard, proposing that not ageing is itself the endpoint, and Peaker refuses it: the FDA needs a measurable functional endpoint like muscle strength, and biological age is not one. On AI in drug discovery Peaker volunteers his own scepticism, saying the gains are marginal against the real cost driver of running clinical trials, and noting that enthusiasm often tracks whose paycheck depends on it.
evidence: Genentech treated as the first biotechnology company, founded in the late 1970s
University and hospital administrative overhead of 30% to 40% charged on top of trial costs
Revolution's pancreatic cancer drug extending survival from about 6 months to about 13
A German lupus study holding B cells undetectable for three to four months, after which autoantibody producing cells largely did not return
A typical tumor carrying several hundred mutations, which is why single mechanism attacks fail
Grapefruit blocking a liver enzyme pathway and disrupting many drugs, an uncontrolled variable in large trials
Eli Lilly described as having conquered the GLP-1 world, with the next wave aimed at preserving muscle mass lost during weight loss
shift: Eisman moves from stated ignorance to a working framework and says so, calling it educational and admitting he learned a ton. What actually changed is his model of failure: he now attributes the Phase 1 to Phase 3 collapse to patient curation rather than to bad science. Peaker does not move at all, because nothing he says is contested on the facts. Neither ends with a stock recommendation.
context: The longest episode in the batch and the show's second sector tutorial in the healthcare arc that began with the UnitedHealth work. It sits apart from the AI capex debate except where Eisman probes whether AI shortens drug development, and Peaker's answer, marginal at best, is a quiet data point against the everything is transformed narrative.

quotes.q: You're still only living for 13 months.
The nirvana for a biotech stock is to have a drug and get it pretty close to the finish line and then have a big pharma take you out.

questions: If B cell reset works across autoimmune disease, which companies capture it and which get bought?
What would make antibiotic development commercially viable, given the drug of last resort trap?
Does GLP-1 muscle preservation create a durable franchise, or a feature Lilly folds into its own products?

title: AI Has a Power Problem: Why the U.S. Power Grid Can't Keep Up | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 69
thesis: Kallo argues that the binding constraint on the entire AI story is no longer chips but electricity and the physical grid, and that the strain predates the data centers now grabbing attention: his own Midtown office already gets curtailment notices on hot days, before any gigawatt-scale data center has even been built. The buildout runs through long, unglamorous pipelines, gas turbines ordered today are not installed at a utility until 2030 or 31, air permits alone take about six months, and high-voltage electrification equipment is scarce, which gives companies like GE Vernova visibility deep into the 2030s and makes nuclear a real but post-2035 earnings story. Grid-scale batteries are the fastest-growing piece, with Tesla's megapack business compounding over 30% a year. On the demand-and-vehicles side he is selective: positive on Tesla via autonomy and a likely SpaceX acquisition, positive on Rivian's cheaper R2, and negative on residential solar, whose door-to-door economics cannot survive 10,000 dollar customer acquisition costs. The final constraint he flags is labor, whether the US can physically staff everything it has committed to build.
pushback: Eisman keeps dragging the conversation from stories to mechanics, summarizing Kallo's turbine timeline as, so you don't build this stuff like tiddlywinks, which Kallo confirms. He also airs the irrational extremes of the substack debate, including the claim that no data centers are being built at all, and asks Kallo to adjudicate. The one open clash is Tesla: Kallo's bull case rests on autonomous vehicles, and Eisman flatly refuses it, noting Musk has promised autonomy for a decade and counting himself a sceptic, while letting Kallo's SpaceX-buys-Tesla call stand as a prediction to monitor.
evidence: The US is adding on the order of 30 gigawatts of power per year, which Eisman likens to building a couple of cities' worth of demand
A gas turbine ordered this quarter will not be built and installed at a utility until about 2030 or 2031
Environmental air permits for new plants take about six months even with federal CO2 rules gone, since hyperscalers keep their own targets
Tesla's megapack grid battery business is growing over 30% a year on the top line, with plants in California, Texas and Shanghai
Residential solar carries customer acquisition costs of about 10,000 dollars per household
Rivian's next-generation R2 SUV targets a price of roughly 40 to 45 thousand dollars
GE Vernova's nuclear business is unlikely to matter to earnings until at least 2035
shift: Eisman fully adopts the power-constraint frame and the long-tailed turbine economics, but the Tesla disagreement ends unresolved: Kallo holds his autonomy-plus-SpaceX thesis, Eisman holds his decade-of-broken-promises scepticism, and both flag labor supply as the next thing to watch.
context: This is the physical-infrastructure leg of the AI capex theme, one ring out from the semiconductor center of the universe Eisman explored with Stacy Rasgon, and the industrial counterpart to Clifton's data-centers-as-new-fracking politics in Ep 67. The multi-year turbine and permitting lags also give the AI trade its long fuse, context for why Eisman keeps saying the capex reckoning is a story for later, not tomorrow.

quotes.q: There haven't really been gigawatt data centers built yet.
Elon's been promising that for 10 years. Count me a skeptic.

questions: Can the US find enough skilled labor to build the plants, turbines and transmission it has already ordered?
If gigawatt data centers have not even arrived yet, how much worse does grid stress get when they do?
Does SpaceX actually buy Tesla, and does that resolve or deepen the governance questions around Musk?

title: Payments Industry - Fear and Reality
thesis: Suchoski's report separates what agentic AI is doing in payments from what investors fear it will do. Today agents handle discovery, search and comparison, while the payment itself is still executed by a human, and even the automated end of the spectrum is nothing more novel than a recurring subscription. Any real agentic commerce still needs what cards already supply, chargeback protection, rewards and universal merchant acceptance, and building that from scratch faces the two sided adoption problem that has killed every challenger network. So agentic payments will most likely run over the existing rails rather than around them, which is exactly what Visa and MasterCard are arranging by partnering with stablecoin issuers. Suchoski adds that some of the selling is not even an opinion on payments, it is investors raising cash to fund faster growing AI names.
pushback: Eisman is the more sceptical party and pushes past Suchoski's careful framing to blunter conclusions. On stablecoins he lets the logic stand and then demands proof, calling adoption glacial and answering the argument with show me the money. On agentic rails he interrupts to explain the consumer protection point himself before Suchoski can, arguing any new rail must replicate what Visa, MasterCard and American Express provide or nobody will use it. He also stops the conversation to explain to listeners that shorting as a source of funds is not the same as a bearish view, and he closes harder than his guest, dismissing Fiserv outright.
evidence: Bitcoin falling from roughly 120,000 near its October peak to about 65,000, hurting stablecoin volumes tied to digital asset trading
Most stablecoin usage still tied to bouncing in and out of crypto positions rather than payments
Visa and MasterCard partnering with stablecoin issuers so wallet holders can spend over existing rails
PayPal still charging premium pricing after Apple Pay and others matched its checkout experience
Toast hit as both a payments and a software name, plus rising memory chip costs, while Micron revenue grows around 200% year over year
Fiserv losing a CEO after only a year, with roughly 20 billion dollars of debt mentioned in the same stretch
The whole group trading down together despite a 2021 stretch when everything went up
shift: Neither moves much, and they converge because they started close. Suchoski stays measured, framing agentic disruption as early and card stickiness as real. Eisman hardens into a rule: only Visa and MasterCard are ownable long term, everything else is a trade. Stablecoins are where he moves most, downgrading them from an interesting growth story to disappointing, and he keeps Fiserv permanently out with a 10 foot pole.
context: This is the show's crypto scepticism and AI disruption threads meeting in one sector. It also inverts the usual AI trade: here AI is not the thing being bought, it is the fear that repriced everything else, and the flows out of payments fund the AI names Eisman holds in his own portfolio. The stablecoin verdict is his most concrete test yet of whether crypto infrastructure ever leaves the trading loop.

quotes.q: Great thesis. Wonderful. Show me the money.
There's habit, there's rewards, and then you have protections.

questions: What evidence would show agents actually executing payments rather than assembling carts?
If cross border B2B is the strongest stablecoin case, what is the specific blocker keeping adoption glacial?
Does the source of funds selling reverse if AI names stall, and does that lift the whole group regardless of fundamentals?

title: The AI Revolution: Who Wins, Who Loses & the SaaSpocalypse  | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 70
thesis: Luria frames the two live debates: whether the data center buildout ever earns a return on the capital pouring into it, and whether anyone in AI has a moat. His answer is that open source eats most of the stack, companies will pay OpenAI or Anthropic for mission-critical work and run free open-source models for everything else, so value accrues to businesses with distribution and infrastructure, Microsoft wins on data centers plus insurmountable Office franchises, Salesforce loses because it stopped investing and just raises prices, and Google is a winner but not the winner, bleeding key researchers to OpenAI. The Oracle episode is his cautionary tale: a backlog jump from 150 to 450 billion dollars in a day turned out to be one deal with an OpenAI that had no money and 1.1 trillion dollars of further commitments. Ives stays the bull: the US leads China in tech for the first time in 30 years, AI creates more jobs than it destroys, cybersecurity budgets double as every agent expands the attack surface, and the industry's real wound is a self-inflicted PR problem of promising to wipe out white-collar jobs while raising electricity bills.
pushback: Eisman announces the structure himself: let me press you both on three counterarguments, capital intensity that has crushed free cash flow, the possibility that there are no moats, and a coming price war as corporations experiment with much cheaper Chinese models. The guests answer that scale itself becomes the moat as hyperscaler data centers compound, but Eisman does not fully buy it, saying in his close that he still has doubts about whether Anthropic or OpenAI have any moat at all, and that the wealth may accrue to the supply chain instead.
evidence: Oracle's backlog jumped from 150 to 450 billion dollars in a single day, later revealed as one OpenAI deal
Beyond its roughly 300 billion dollar Oracle commitment, OpenAI made about 1.1 trillion dollars of additional commitments without the capital to fund them
Oracle traded around 350 intraday at the peak of the backlog euphoria before the market reassessed
Cybersecurity budgets are expected to roughly double over the next two to three years as AI agents multiply the attack surface
A Google researcher described as one of the inventors of modern AI has left for OpenAI, evidence of Google's internal bureaucracy problem
Google sits a distant second in consumer chat and roughly third in enterprise AI, a winner but not the winner
shift: The guests remain long-term bulls but openly concede what would have been unthinkable a year earlier: the debate now has a respectable bear case built on capital intensity, missing moats and price war risk. Eisman ends persuaded on the breadth of supply chain wealth creation, unpersuaded on model-company moats, and both sides agree to reconvene in the fall because the thesis changes weekly.
context: This is the centerpiece of the show's AI capex and returns theme, giving names and mechanisms to the SaaSpocalypse Eisman tracks weekly through ServiceNow, IBM and Equifax in the wraps. The Oracle-OpenAI circularity story becomes the show's standing exhibit for what a reckoning looks like, echoed in the August 14 wrap's claim that everything hinges on Anthropic and OpenAI.

quotes.q: For the first time in 30 years, the US is ahead of China when it comes to tech.
They made an additional 1.1 trillion dollars of commitments without having any money.

questions: If open source takes everything but mission-critical workloads, what revenue base ever justifies the model companies' commitments?
Do hyperscaler data centers really constitute a moat, or just a shared cost of staying in the game?
How quickly could cheap Chinese models turn subsidized token pricing into a full price war?

title: The Real Estate Brokerage War, For-Profit Education, & the Art of the Short with Brad Safalow
thesis: Safalow argues the residential brokerage industry looks chaotic but has barely changed where it counts. Commissions still sit at 5 to 5.2 percent, for sale by owner share has not moved, and the brokerage value proposition is still marketing, technology, back office and brand. The real fight is over the MLS itself, where Compass is pushing private listings and building a national MLS equivalent it would steer, and where states are now legislating against it faster than the industry can move. He stays long Zillow on the view that it remains ground central for the whole ecosystem even after a violent re-rating. On the short side he reads for-profit education as structurally impaired by fewer high school students, the loss of Grad Plus, and AI collapsing the cost of educational content, and he updates three single name shorts where the thesis is deterioration nobody has marked yet.
pushback: Eisman keeps dragging the conversation out of the weeds and back to mechanics, stopping Safalow to define MLS, private listings and FSBO before letting the argument continue. He tests the disruption story directly and gets Safalow to concede a lot of noise and not a lot of change. In the wrap he splits from his guest in one place, saying Compass's attempt to circumvent the MLS does not sound successful while noting that Safalow, who owns the pain, still likes Zillow after the stock hurt him.
evidence: National commission steady between 5 and 5.2 percent, split roughly 2.5 percent to each side, with brokers returning about 80 percent to the agent
Roughly 500 MLSs in the country, which Safalow says is far too many
Washington's private listing ban taking effect and Connecticut proposing rules, both within four to eight weeks of taping
Transaction volume expected in high single digits to low double digits for the year
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminating Grad Plus, which let graduate students borrow to cost of attendance
Costco going from zero to more than 10 percent of Fresh Pet revenue between 2022 and 2025, with Costco and Walmart the sole sources of growth
Kinsale trading at three and a half to four times book with earnings estimates Safalow believes are 40 to 60 percent too high
shift: Nothing converges and nothing needs to. Safalow holds Zillow long and all three prior shorts, Eisman accepts the short cases and records his own doubt about Compass's ability to route around the MLS, and both end where they started on for-profit education being uninvestable on the long side.
context: This is the show's housing affordability thread approached through the plumbing rather than the price. It also sits inside the running AI capex and returns argument, since Safalow reads Google's spending as a scorched earth bid to outlast Meta and Microsoft while being short the stock, and inside Eisman's habit of treating industries run by bad people as a permanent short bias.

quotes.q: It's a stock that I've been recommending, and it's been nothing short of a disaster for me personally.
So a lot of noise, not a lot of change.

questions: If state legislatures keep banning private listings, does Compass have a business model left that is not leverage?
What breaks the Trupanion spiral other than repricing an aging book that cannot be regrown?
Does AI lower the cost of educational content enough to impair non-profit higher education too, and what is the tradable expression?

title: 250 Years of American Capitalism: Hamilton, the GFC, & the AI Boom | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 71
thesis: Wooldridge, Alan Greenspan's co-author on Capitalism in America, argues the through-line of US economic history is that America embraced creative destruction on a bigger scale and with more enthusiasm than any other country. The preconditions were structural: a massive internal market, a constitution that constrains government and frees markets, and a self-selected population wired toward ambition, all built on Hamilton's victory over Jefferson, including the infant-industry tariffs that let American manufacturing grow strong enough to face Britain. The busts are part of the same machine, and policy can make them worse: the Depression deepened partly because the roughly six-month Hoover-to-FDR handover left the country effectively without a government mid-calamity, and before the GFC finance had become untethered from the real economy, self-serving and absorbing too much talent and capital. His closing ledger is optimism about a culture where genius expresses itself by building companies, set against political instability, creeping corporatism and unnecessary corporate concentration.
pushback: The real collision is over the GFC. Eisman extracts the admission that Greenspan wrote the book's GFC section entirely solo, then asks what Greenspan believed caused the crisis; the answer, that Greenspan mostly blamed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, is exactly the exculpatory account Eisman spent his career against, and he says on air that he disagrees, locating the cause in the excess leverage Greenspan himself allowed into the banking system.
evidence: The book is Capitalism in America by Alan Greenspan and Adrian Wooldridge, revisited for the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence
Hamilton's infant-industry tariff argument was later adopted by Germany, and protected industries in both countries grew into dominant ones
The Hoover-to-FDR transition took about six months, leaving no effective government in the middle of the Depression
Greenspan wrote the book's Great Financial Crisis section solo and placed most blame on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
Wooldridge and Greenspan argue pre-GFC finance had become self-serving, absorbing too much of the economy's talent and investment
Wooldridge's worry list for America: political instability, creeping corporatism, politicians interfering with business, and excessive corporate concentration
shift: Nothing converges on the GFC: Wooldridge faithfully reports Greenspan's Fannie-and-Freddie account, Eisman states his leverage counter-thesis and lets the disagreement stand, while warmly recommending the book. The shared ground is the creative destruction frame, which Eisman clearly enjoys as history and as an implicit argument about the AI boom.
context: A deliberate step back from the weekly AI grind, this episode gives the show its longest lens: booms, busts and infant industries as the normal metabolism of American capitalism, with obvious echoes for the AI capex debate and Eisman's own reading-is-my-superpower theme from the July wraps. The GFC exchange is also the series' most direct confrontation between Eisman's Big Short history and the official Greenspan account.

quotes.q: In America, an expression of genius is to build a great company, and to keep that great company going.
I think it was much more to do with the excess leverage that Greenspan allowed into the banking system.

questions: If busts are the price of creative destruction, which kind of bust does the AI buildout most resemble, railroads, housing or something new?
Does today's corporate concentration break the historical pattern of American turnover that Wooldridge credits for its dynamism?
Would Greenspan's Fannie-and-Freddie account of the GFC survive the disclosure standards Eisman demands of companies today?

title: Streaming Hits Hollywood Hard: Here's Why with Producer Peter Hoffman
thesis: Eisman's frame is a margin story. Television and film used to earn twice, once on first run and again on repeated syndication sales, and the incumbents traded that away by selling their libraries to Netflix until Netflix could fund its own hits. Streaming replaced it with a structurally lower margin business that supports only a handful of players, and it is already maturing. Hoffman supplies the production side of the same collapse: independents once financed films on presales against foreign rights and presaleable talent, which let them make pictures the studios would not, and that financing machinery is gone. What remains is a small set of proven creators who get funded and everyone else who does not.
pushback: Eisman does not argue with Hoffman so much as press him on the unanswerable. He asks why Angel Heart failed despite being, in his own account, so good he and his friends walked out speechless, and whether film outcomes can be predicted at all. Hoffman refuses the flattering answer and says nobody knows. Eisman also presses on why Neuromancer resisted Hoffman for nearly 15 years and Apple could simply make it, forcing the plain answer that Apple has the money and does not need to presell anything.
evidence: Netflix earnings per share growth of 11 percent in the most recent quarter against 47 percent in the second quarter of 2025, with the stock down 25 percent on the year
Disney's share price back where it sat in late 2014, about 12 years of no return
AMC at roughly 10 dollars against 80 dollars ten years earlier
Prime Video at about 2 percent of Amazon revenue, YouTube at about 15 percent of Google
Hoffman stopping a James Cameron picture at 30 days over schedule, and the rule that a director who shot 90 percent of a film cannot remove his credit
New Orleans film production falling from about 1.2 billion dollars in the year of Hoffman's indictment to about 200 million the next year, with Georgia now at about 2 billion
shift: Nothing moves, because the two are describing the same decline from opposite ends. Eisman keeps the financial frame that streaming is a maturing lower margin business, Hoffman keeps the craft frame that the financing that funded risk is gone, and neither disputes the other.
context: One of the show's clearest illustrations of a K-shaped outcome inside a single industry: Netflix and the balance sheet buyers on one side, everyone dependent on presales on the other. It also serves as Eisman's standing warning about incumbents monetizing an asset today at the cost of the franchise, and it sets up the Paramount and Warner Bros thread he returns to three weeks later.

quotes.q: We will hang the capitalists with the rope they will sell us.
Apple is like the studios. They have the money. They decide to make it. They spend the money.

questions: If streaming supports only a few players, which of the legacy transitions gets abandoned rather than completed?
Does anything replace presale financing for films that lack presaleable talent, or does that category simply stop existing?
How much of a state's production base is really policy-driven rather than sticky, given how fast New Orleans emptied into Georgia?

title: Private Credit's Clock is Ticking w/ Glenn Schorr & Ken Worthington | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 72
thesis: Recorded the morning after Microsoft soared and Meta cratered, the conversation builds a two-speed picture of financial services. In private markets, monetization timelines have stretched enormously, roughly seven years even with record equity markets and a better IPO window, some sponsors have already handed lenders the keys rather than inject more equity, and the real test of private credit's software overexposure only arrives with next year's refinancing wall, when much lower valuations meet maturing debt. Meanwhile the public side is humming: trading thrives on disagreement, and banks and brokers are printing records. Worthington adds the digital layer: blockchains and tokens proliferate, venues like Coinbase benefit, and stablecoins plausibly become the settlement layer for 24/7 trading, but agentic AI money management is premature because internal studies show the agents are wrong most of the time, telling investors what they want to hear.
pushback: The sharpest moment is Eisman's Bitcoin cross-examination: after Worthington lays out the token proliferation thesis, Eisman grants every word of it and then asks, twice, what any of it has to do with owning Bitcoin, and Worthington has no strong answer. Eisman is also openly more negative on private credit than either guest, and he flips their good news at the end, noting that when everything in the investment banks is humming is precisely when he starts to worry.
evidence: Microsoft rose over 10% on results while Meta fell about 10% on 28% revenue growth against 55% expense growth
Situational Awareness, a 20 billion dollar hedge fund run by a former OpenAI employee, was liquidated after leveraged AI losses
Private equity monetization timelines have lengthened dramatically, even as KKR posted record monetizations in the same quarter
In extreme cases sponsors have handed the keys to lenders rather than put fresh equity into struggling software borrowers
Equity trading revenues rose about 68% on volume growth of only 9 to 10%, with margin balances up about 50%
Internal studies at JP Morgan found AI agents managing money are wrong the majority of the time, echoing user prompts rather than optimizing portfolios
shift: Worthington effectively concedes the Bitcoin point, holding his blockchain infrastructure thesis while admitting he lacks a case for the coin itself. On private credit, nobody moves: the guests stay constructive, Eisman keeps his doubts, and all three agree the verdict waits for the software refinancings early next year.
context: This is the show's most direct treatment of its private credit theme, putting a date, early next year's software refinancing wall, on the risk Slok quantified via debt vintages in Ep 68. The Bitcoin exchange extends the running crypto scepticism from the Circle collapse coverage and the Kalshi thesis, and the humming-banks unease sets up Verrone's new-highs observation in Ep 73.

quotes.q: When everybody agrees on something, trading's not going to be so good.
I grant you everything you just said. Everything. What's that got to do with Bitcoin?

questions: How many software borrowers survive next year's refinancings when lenders demand fresh equity at today's lower valuations?
If AI agents are wrong most of the time managing money, what has to change before banks let them touch client cash?
Can stablecoins become the settlement layer for 24/7 trading without Visa and Mastercard controlling the rails?

title: Why the Iran War Is Stuck & What Comes Next with Steven Cook
thesis: Cook argues the war produced a massive tactical success and a strategic dead end. Israel decapitated the Iranian leadership in the opening minutes, which removed both the target set and the counterparty the president hoped to pluck out and deal with. Iran had spent the nine months since the earlier strikes dispersing missiles and decentralizing command and control, so heavy damage did not stop it firing at Israel and then at the Gulf states, and the Strait blockade turned a military campaign into an economic one the president would not pay for. Because the regime prioritizes survival over the economy, the pressure that was supposed to force capitulation simply does not bite. Cook's forecast is continuation: low level violence in the Strait, intermittent bombing, and no negotiation.
pushback: Eisman refuses the diplomacy premise. He sets the Strait aside as technically solvable and puts the real question as nuclear fuel, then asks why anyone would believe an Iranian signature on paper. Cook does not defend the deal, answering that he does not know and pointing back to the same doubt that surrounded the 2015 agreement. Eisman also pushes Cook to name what kind of regime accepts economic collapse, and Cook accepts the framing that this is not a normal regime.
evidence: 40 of Iran's top leaders killed in the first minutes of the Israeli operation
Nine months between the June 2025 Operation Midnight Hammer and the later Israeli campaign, used to distribute missile capability and decentralize command
Iranian strikes on the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Oman, including Dubai Airport, data centers and Amazon web services facilities
The president calling off the campaign in early April, with the Strait of Hormuz still closed at taping on July 28
Israeli withdrawal from two Lebanese villages handed to the Lebanese armed forces under a United States monitored framework
Cook seeing no woman on a 2002 trip to Saudi Arabia until he sat outside a Riyadh Prada on his last day
shift: Nothing shifts, and both say so. Cook holds that the stalemate persists and predicts the same conversation in three or four months, Eisman ends agreeing that things will be ugly for a while because Iran wants power rather than a deal.
context: Iran is the macro overhang the Weekly Wrap has carried for months, and this is Eisman's attempt to price the geopolitics rather than react to headlines. A closed Strait feeds straight into the energy and inflation questions that govern his read on the Fed, and Cook's Gulf detail, including strikes on data centers and cloud facilities, ties the war to the AI buildout the show tracks elsewhere.

quotes.q: As long as the leadership remained in power and alive, that's all that they really cared about.
Why would you trust the Iranians at all on that subject?

questions: What actually reopens the Strait if neither escalation nor negotiation has moved it since April?
Can a nuclear agreement be verified at all once the officials who would sign it have been killed?
Does the Lebanon framework survive first contact with Hezbollah refusing to disarm?

title: The AI Trade, Rising Rates, and Why the Market Is Still Standing | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 73
thesis: Trennert sees a gathering storm, war, resurgent tariffs, the hyperscaler capex debate and a Fed remaking itself under Warsh, and worries chiefly about concentration in the top ten names. Verrone answers with the internals: even as the index churned for eight weeks and semis corrected, the share of S&P stocks above their 200-day average rose from about 50% in early June to 75%, a rotational tape that keeps repairing itself. Their old rule that a 4.5% ten-year would pull money out of equities has simply failed, so the threshold must be higher than most people think, and until yields find it the bull market stands. Around that core they argue private credit was largely a regulatory arbitrage against Dodd-Frank-constrained banks, that traditional asset managers now outperform private equity stocks as the zero-rate subsidy unwinds, and that worldwide bank stocks at new highs are inconsistent with an imminent crisis. The Warsh Fed's retreat from forward guidance means more volatility, which Trennert regards as healthy discipline rather than danger.
pushback: Eisman keeps demanding the number: if 4.5% on the ten-year did not break the market, what does, and Verrone concedes he can only say higher than most people think. Eisman pushes Verrone for a verdict on Meta's ugly quarter and gets a candid no strong view, just the reminder that the stock's 2022 collapse is what forced Zuckerberg to change course. He also draws out the tension in their own bullishness, that private equity was the single greatest beneficiary of zero rates, seven-year monetization timelines and all, yet the market is being led by the traditional managers instead.
evidence: About 50% of S&P stocks were above their 200-day average on June 2 versus 75% at recording, improvement during a churning tape
The old assumption that a 4.5% ten-year yield would pull money from equities has failed, and the true threshold is unknown but higher
Private equity monetization timelines now run about seven years
Regulated utilities have traded poorly all year despite the AI power theme running through the sector
Meta bottomed near 90 dollars in late 2022 before Zuckerberg reversed course on metaverse spending
Money managers from State Street to T. Rowe to Invesco are leading the asset management group, outperforming private equity stocks
shift: Eisman comes away more constructive than he arrived: his stated takeaway is that the economy is quite strong, and that absent a much bigger yield spike or an AI breakdown, Trennert and Verrone are effectively bullish through year-end. The guests hold their one confession of ignorance, nobody knows the rate that finally matters, and Trennert holds his welcome-the-volatility read of the Warsh Fed.
context: The season-closing temperature check before the two-week break, it stitches together the show's threads: the concentration risk from the Sohn episode, the private credit as regulatory arb argument that complements Ep 72, and the banks and Fed theme now centered on Warsh killing forward guidance. Verrone's every-bank-at-new-highs observation directly answers the crisis-hunting instinct Eisman confessed to in the July 17 wrap.

quotes.q: I can't think of too many times where you're on the verge of a big problem and every bank stock is at new highs.
I can't think of an industry that benefited more from near zero percent interest rates than private equity.

questions: What ten-year yield finally makes bonds compelling enough to break the equity market's internals?
Is the rotation beneath the index genuine broadening or just the AI theme migrating between sectors?
Does a Fed without forward guidance produce healthy discipline or the policy accident the whiners fear?

title: Why Europe Can't Fix Itself & Why It's Getting Worse with Wolfgang Munchau
thesis: Munchau's argument is that Europe's stagnation is not cyclical and not fixable with the usual levers. Germany led global technology until the 1980s and 1990s and then stopped innovating, extending nineteenth century breakthroughs in chemistry and engineering into a car industry that carried the whole economy through suppliers and finance. That engine is now losing to China with no diversification plan, and the reflex is to subsidize the car industry rather than replace it. Europe compounded the problem by choosing to regulate digital industries it never participated in, starting with GDPR. Underneath all of it is a political structure Munchau likens to a confederacy that refuses to become a federal state, so even correct diagnoses cannot become decisions.
pushback: Eisman tests whether the problem is fixable by policy and gets told it is not. He says plainly that the conversation is depressing, because a story about tax cuts and regulatory burden would have an answer and a story about culture does not, and he adds that he does not think anybody knows how to solve a culture problem. He also interrupts to check a hard number, asking whether German GDP has simply not grown in three to four years, and Munchau substitutes the sharper statistic that productivity has been flat for eight.
evidence: German productivity flat for eight years, with 2018 as the peak and industry falling over the period
GDPR named as the first of the big European tech regulations and the origin of the cookie banners
The UK the most active AI investor in Europe, with spinoffs around its London AI cluster, against small scenes in Munich and Paris and almost nothing in Italy or Spain
Munchau's attribution of American technology scale to capital markets rather than tax breaks
German coal likely to run longer than planned because nuclear was switched off
France unable to touch pensions and Germany unable to touch welfare while defense spending must rise, producing debt build up across every European country
shift: Nothing shifts, and the movement is downward rather than toward agreement. Munchau came to report deterioration and reports it, Eisman arrives looking for a policy fix and leaves calling the situation sad and pretty hopeless.
context: This is the counterweight to the show's American AI capex debate. Where Eisman worries that United States hyperscalers are overspending, Munchau's Europe is the control case for underspending, and it argues that the returns question is a luxury only a region with capital markets gets to ask. The fighter jet anecdote Eisman highlights, where a Franco German program collapsed because Germany could not politically accept building in France, is the whole thesis in one story.

quotes.q: They could regulate the tech industry, which was a stupidity, a sound of arrogance.
This is a culture problem. And culture problem, I don't know how to solve a culture problem.

questions: What tipping point would force restructuring, given Munchau says anger is rising but the point is not close?
Can the UK cluster reach a scale that matters without European capital markets behind it?
If subsidy is the reflex for every failing sector, where does the fiscal room come from once debt is already exploding?

title: The Juiciest Corporate Scandals with Becca Platsky
thesis: Platsky's premise is that corporate fraud is a people story hidden behind formal disclosure, and that the tell is usually a mismatch between what a company says on television and what it reports. She works the Charlie Javice case as the model: a product that automated student aid claiming 400,000 users with extraordinarily valuable personal data, banks that passed, and JPMorgan that bought. The court held that JPMorgan's diligence was not on trial, which Eisman endorses on the principle that the buyer's stupidity is not a defense for the seller. From there she extends the pattern to Paramount governance, prediction markets with no functioning regulator, and FIFA sponsorship money going straight into executives' pockets.
pushback: The real disagreement is about human nature. Platsky raises the humility argument, that fraud can happen to anybody and good people can cross the line, and asks whether Eisman has ever felt that pull. He rejects it outright, saying somebody who does something illegal always did things illegal and that Javice was guaranteed doing bad things before. Platsky says only that it is interesting and does not concede. She also pushes back on his media consolidation view, arguing that one family owning Paramount, CBS, CNN by way of Warner Bros and TikTok is a diversity of news problem, while he answers that nobody cares about traditional media any more.
evidence: Frank pitched as 400,000 users with socials, parental income, schools, majors, emails, home addresses and phone numbers
Multiple name brand banks declining before JPMorgan bought
The JPMorgan executive who ran the diligence, once in conversation to replace Jamie Dimon, since demoted
A teleprompter technician for Trump's speeches betting on which words he would say in prediction markets
Polymarket defending itself to the CFTC on the ground that it is an innovative company
Chuck Blazer of FIFA keeping an 8,000 dollar a month Trump Tower apartment plus a 6,000 dollar a month apartment for his cats and parents
No executive prosecuted or, by Eisman's account, even investigated by the Justice Department after 2008
shift: Neither budges on the character question and both end in the same place on remedy. Platsky asks three times what an ordinary person can do, and Eisman offers nothing beyond whistleblowing, which they agree can destroy your life, so she lands on shrinking your circle and managing the anger.
context: This is Eisman's founding grievance restated for a new audience, that 2008 was the largest fraud in history and produced no investigation, and he explicitly says the laws were already there. It also folds into two live show themes: his preference for Paramount and Warner Bros merging so Netflix does not own the entire content business, and his crypto and event market scepticism, here aimed at venues that let insiders trade on information with no regulator in place.

quotes.q: You being stupid is not a defense for somebody else to take advantage of you.
Frauds can't last a hell of a lot longer than you.

questions: If the statutes already exist, what changed inside the Justice Department that made 2008 unprosecutable?
Does the CFTC settle the event contract question before or after the first market-moving insider case?
Is Eisman's rule that fraudsters always offended before a real base rate or a survivorship artifact of the cases that get caught?

title: The Art of the Short with Lakshmi Ganapathi: FICO, DoorDash, and AeroVironment
thesis: Ganapathi argues FICO has shattered its own monopoly by raising prices about 1,600%, angering the mortgage ecosystem and giving the FHFA reason to push VantageScore. Management first dismissed Vantage at about 2% share, then cited roughly 20 to 25%, which tells her it was caught off guard. She does not expect FICO to vanish, only to lose its authority, and sets a target under 500. AeroVironment is priced out of its own market by far cheaper drones, and DoorDash faces European lawsuits plus demand propped up by buy now, pay later credit.
pushback: Eisman presses DoorDash on timing: the stretched consumer keeps paying, which hurts the thesis for now. Ganapathi concedes the pattern has run since 2020 and refuses to predict a collapse, calling the strain persistent and prolonged. He also doubts sell-side share data; she says to add plus or minus 10 to any number.
evidence: FICO raised prices about 1,600% over four to five years
FICO stock a little over 1,000 against her target under 500
Kelsey Zhu's latest figure for Vantage-scored securitized mortgages was about 8%, against about 2% the prior month
Vantage says it can score 33 to 37 million people FICO cannot
AeroVironment, market cap about 9 to 10 billion, sells drones at 50,000 dollars plus against rivals at 5,000 or less
France criminally convicted Deliveroo, with suspended sentences for two former general managers
shift: Eisman stays short FICO and grows more confident. He is tempted to short AeroVironment but holds off over volatility. He accepts the DoorDash consumer credit logic while Ganapathi gives no date for it.
context: FICO is his one disclosed short, and this episode reinforces it with fresh share data. The DoorDash credit argument extends Ganapathi's earlier call of a consumer crack, which he accepted as direction but not as date.

quotes.q: I would always add like plus or minus 10 with whatever number that comes out.
It looks like, at least to me, that FICO is on the verge of losing its monopoly.

questions: Does VantageScore's share of securitized mortgages keep rising now that it is open to all lenders?
What would force a pullback in buy now, pay later credit to DoorDash users?
Can AeroVironment close the price gap with low-cost drone makers?

title: P&C Stocks Worth Owning: The AI Hedge with Ryan Tunis | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 74
thesis: Tunis argues property and casualty insurance runs on its own pricing cycle, which makes it a place to hide when investors want stability over growth. Commercial lines are about a year into a soft market that is spreading into casualty, so buying on business mix no longer works. He prefers self-help, chiefly AIG near book value, plus Travelers and the reinsurance brokers. Personal auto faces a slower threat as car technology cuts accident rates and shrinks the market.
pushback: Eisman is more negative than Tunis on Trupanion, calling it a bad business despite being a satisfied customer. He questions whether reinsurers are franchises, and Tunis concedes the industry has accepted unacceptable returns. On Kinsale, Eisman says its approach sounds dishonest; Tunis defends its mid-50s loss ratios but flags low broker pay as a soft market risk.
evidence: The commercial soft market is about a year old
Tunis recommends Travelers and AIG, not Chubb
AIG trades around book value
Trupanion policies cost about 1,000 dollars a year, with free cash flow near 2% of revenue, about 30 to 40 million
Kinsale's loss ratios sit in the mid-50s
Reinsurance brokers are his top subgroup
shift: Eisman leaves more negative on personal lines than he arrived. He sees little to do yet in brokers, stays extremely negative on Trupanion and sees Kinsale as potentially problematic, while Tunis calls it a good company.
context: The first property and casualty deep dive on the show, framed as a hedge against the AI trade he worries about in the same week. It bears on two holdings: AIG, which Tunis backs, and Progressive, whose personal lines business Eisman now views more warily.

quotes.q: We've seen this industry willing to accept returns that are unacceptable.
I have no complaints about Trupanion as a company. I just think it's a bad business.

questions: How long can the commercial soft market last?
Will falling accident rates cut Progressive's growth more than its margins?
How does Kinsale perform in its first real soft market?

title: Inside AI’s Fragile Ecosystem with Ed Zitron
thesis: Zitron argues AI revenue is small against more than a trillion dollars of hyperscaler capex, and most of it comes from OpenAI and Anthropic, which lose heavily and depend on constant fundraising. Hyperscalers spend to capture revenue from two labs they must keep inflating, while Nvidia funds customers who buy its chips. Heavily subsidized subscriptions and a token maxing boom flattered growth, and enterprises are now cutting costs. Data center buildouts are slower and harder than assumed, so the chain faces both a funding wall and a physical one.
pushback: Eisman does not dispute the numbers but challenges the premise: these companies are not run by idiots, so how could they be in a mania? Zitron traces it to the zero-rate boom of 2021, and Eisman answers with the GFC, where Wall Street could not stop until subprime blew up. Eisman also frames Zitron's OpenAI view as preparing for failure, not predicting it.
evidence: Microsoft's fiscal 2026 AI revenue was 34.33 billion, 24.1 billion from OpenAI, per a Bloomberg estimate
OpenAI lost 20.9 billion on 13.07 billion of revenue in 2025
OpenAI's latest quarterly operating margin was about minus 183%
110 billion of OpenAI's 122 billion raise came from Amazon, SoftBank and Nvidia
OpenAI subscriptions let users burn about 14,000 dollars of compute for 200 dollars
About 70% of hyperscaler AI revenue comes from the two labs, about 25 to 35% of cloud revenue
shift: Eisman ends aligned with Zitron. He calls the dependence on the two labs nerve-wracking and names OpenAI the problem child, while Zitron holds that none of the spending is worth it. Eisman stops short of calling a bubble.
context: This sharpens his long-held top AI risk, dependence on Anthropic and OpenAI, into a specific claim that OpenAI is the weaker lab. It follows the Anthropic S-1 question and his sales of Oracle and Meta over capital intensity.

quotes.q: They're doing it so they can capture revenue from two companies that they themselves have to keep inflating.

questions: What will Anthropic's S-1 show for second-half 2026 revenue after token maxing faded?
Can OpenAI keep raising money as its press sours?
How much of Oracle's 600 billion backlog survives an OpenAI funding failure?

title: The Big Short Partners Reunite: Rates, AI, Gold and Two Stock Picks | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 75
thesis: Collins argues the US fiscal position has passed the point of repair: interest expense plus entitlements run at about 110% of tax receipts, interest cannot be cut, entitlements will not be, and big tax increases will not happen under this administration. That leaves printing, which is why he holds more conviction in precious metals than in anything for years. Gold is a debt-free asset that central banks, China included, keep adding, while Treasuries are someone else's liability. Bessent's bond buying and pressure for lower rates are a six-to-nine-month bet that growth slows enough to cool inflation, played with signaling games in the interim.
pushback: Eisman makes Collins explain the link between rates and gold for viewers who do not see it, and presses on why the Treasury needs six to nine months. The partners in turn push Eisman to concede that the deficit hawks were right once promised fraud cuts came to almost nothing; the answer comes back that the old deficit view still holds, argued less passionately than before. On Carvana the group agrees profits look enhanced but accepts that proving it has been impossible for eight years.
evidence: Interest expense plus entitlements at about 110% of tax receipts
Bessent's initial long-bond purchase of at least 4 billion dollars
Citadel illustrated with about 25 billion of capital running roughly 125 billion of positions at five to one
Carvana at about 30 to 40 times earnings
Cannabis selling for about 200 dollars a pound in California, with 50% to 65% EBITDA margins possible abroad
All three are short FICO
shift: Little moves. Eisman and his partners agree on FICO, on the futility of Treasury intervention and on AI nerves. The partners hold their gold conviction; Eisman asks questions rather than taking a position on metals.
context: The first conversation with his old partners since the show's launch in April 2025, and it anchors the September theme of a rising long end he no longer thinks the market can ignore. It restates his FICO short, and the unnamed cannabis pick appears to be Glass House Brands, his own speculative holding, now tied to a 2027 catalyst.

quotes.q: I think I've had as much conviction in this precious metals trade as I've had in anything in a long, long time.

questions: Can Treasury buy enough long bonds to matter without an alternative buyer?
Does the cannabis margin case survive if interstate or overseas sales slip past 2027?

title: How to Analyze Bank Stocks (Part 1): Leverage, Accounting, and Loan Losses
thesis: Banking is a low-margin business, so a bank earns an adequate return only by putting its ROA through leverage: ROE equals ROA times leverage. That same arithmetic gives managements an incentive to lever up, which is why regulators set capital ratios, and why risk weighting invites banks to stuff balance sheets with low-weighted assets. Risk weights rest on loss history, but loss history depends on underwriting that can loosen. Because CECL forces reserve true-ups at once, provisions become the variable investors fear most, and the non-accrual data at the four largest banks becomes the best window on credit.
